+
+## The blog post
+
+# The shape of the book, not its size: what confidential transfers on the XRP Ledger hide
+
+*Status, before anything else: this is a research project on the XRP Ledger's
+Devnet test network. It is not audited, not production-ready, and not safe to put
+value behind. Its signer refuses every network but Devnet.*
+
+Can a token move confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, under a standard called
+XLS-96, and today only on Devnet. Read on 2026-10-22 at 03:25 UTC, its amendment,
+`ConfidentialTransfer`, was enabled on Devnet, and supported but not enabled on
+Mainnet and Testnet. That reading goes stale. The repository has a script that
+takes a fresh one.
+
+What XLS-96 hides is narrower than the word *confidential* suggests. It hides
+balances, and the amounts of transfers between confidential balances. It does not
+hide who pays whom, when, or how often. It does not hide amounts entering or
+leaving confidential form. And it hides nothing from the token's issuer.
+
+Since mid-August I have been building an application on it to find out exactly
+where that line falls, by running transactions rather than by reading the
+specification. This post is what I found, what the reviews of my own work caught,
+and what went back upstream. The project is called W-CONF. The code and its claims
+register are public at
+[github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions](https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions),
+and a read-only demo is at
+[xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app](https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app).
+
+Ids such as *E-58* in this post are rows in the project's claims register,
+[`CLAIMS.md`](https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions/blob/main/CLAIMS.md).
+Each row says what supports it. Where this post and a row disagree, the row wins.
+
+I built it with Claude Code as the coding agent. The reviews described below were
+run by other models (Codex and Gemini) and by separate Claude sessions, each given
+a different packet.
+
+* * *
+
+## What XLS-96 is, briefly
+
+The XRP Ledger is public: anyone can read every account and every transaction.
+Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs, XLS-33) are one of its token types. XLS-96,
+Confidential Transfers for MPTs, lets a holder keep an MPT balance encrypted on
+that public ledger.
+
+Each confidential balance is an ElGamal ciphertext. A holder registers their own
+encryption key when they opt in. The ledger still has to stop anyone spending more
+than they hold, so every transaction that spends from a confidential balance
+carries zero-knowledge proofs, which validators check without learning the
+amount.
+
+A position moves through four transactions:
+
+- **Convert** moves tokens from a public balance into confidential form. The
+  amount is published.
+- **Send** moves an amount from one confidential balance to another. The amount is
+  hidden. The sender and receiver are not.
+- **MergeInbox** moves what a holder has received into the balance they can spend.
+- **ConvertBack** moves tokens back to a public balance. The amount is published.
+
+Only Send hides an amount.
+
+The specification, XLS-0096, is the work of Murat Cenk, Aanchal Malhotra, Ayo
+Akinyele, Peter Chen, Shawn Xie and Yinyi Qian, and has been `Final` since
+2026-09-03 (E-1). The compact sigma protocol behind its send proof is the work of
+Tess Dore and Murat Cenk at RippleX Research. The reference cryptography is
+[`XRPLF/mpt-crypto`](https://github.com/XRPLF/mpt-crypto). This project builds on
+their work and claims none of it.
+
+* * *
+
+## What it hides, and what it does not
+
+**Hidden from the public:** each holder's balance, and the amount of each Send.
+
+**Public, always:**
+
+- The sender and receiver of every transfer, and when it happened, so how often
+  anyone transacts (P-4, P-11).
+- Every amount converted in or out, each one separately.
+- The token's total supply, and the total held in confidential form.
+- That a balance is exactly zero, in three cases, below.
+
+**Who can read every balance:** the issuer, always. XLS-96 keeps a second copy of
+each confidential balance, encrypted to the issuer's key, and no setting turns it
+off (P-9). An auditor can read them too, if the token names one, and only one is
+supported (E-11). I ran this rather than inferring it. The holder, the issuer and
+the auditor each decrypted the same balance, 500, and each read 475 after a
+25-unit Send (E-58).
+
+**Who can spend:** only whoever holds the holder's encryption secret, because a
+Send's proof cannot be made without it (E-33). Where that secret is derived from
+the account's master seed, as this project derives it, whoever holds the seed
+holds the secret too. The issuer cannot spend a holder's balance. If the token
+allows clawback, the issuer can destroy it, crediting no one, and this project's
+tokens allow clawback (E-12). Unless the token's flags were made unchangeable when
+it was created, the issuer can also turn on locking later and freeze balances.
+That second power I read in rippled's source and did not run (E-290).
+
+**Zero is sometimes visible.** XLS-96 writes a fixed encryption of zero, which
+anyone can recompute from public inputs, in three places: a new confidential
+balance, an inbox that a MergeInbox has just emptied, and a position clawed back.
+So enrolment is publicly visible. The English documentation said this value could
+not be told apart from other ciphertexts. I recomputed it from public inputs and
+matched it byte for byte against live Devnet state (F-1, E-59), reported it, and
+the English page was corrected in September. A balance spent down to zero holds a
+randomised encryption of zero, and is not recognisable (E-211).
+
+**The public numbers bound the hidden ones.** If a holder converts in 500, receives
+nothing, and converts back 400, anyone can work out that the other 100 is either
+still held or has left by confidential Send. No key is needed. I first wrote that
+the 100 *"left by transfer"*. That overstated what an observer learns, and it is
+recorded as a correction (R-7).
+
+* * *
+
+## No rotation, no recovery
+
+A registered key can never be changed (E-9). XLS-96 has no key rotation and no key
+recovery (P-10). If a holder loses their key, and any seed it could be re-derived
+from, the balance cannot be spent. The only remedy is an issuer clawback, which
+destroys the balance.
+
+A draft standard, XLS-99, by Aanchal Malhotra and Yinyi Qian, proposes rotation for
+holder, issuer and auditor keys, and recovery from key loss. On 2026-10-22,
+rippled's development branch and its release candidate `3.5.0-rc1` declared its
+amendment as not supported, and Mainnet, Testnet and Devnet did not know it (E-353).
+So there is no rotation or recovery in XLS-96, or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet,
+today.
+
+* * *
+
+## The example: a confidential receivables facility
+
+To test the standard against something with stakes, I built the core of a
+receivables facility. A bank pays a large buyer's suppliers early, against their
+invoices. How much a supplier draws says a lot about its cash position, so these
+amounts are commercially sensitive.
+
+The bank issues a token. A Dedicated Account, an ordinary XRPL account, holds the
+float and converts it into confidential form once. Suppliers enrol, draw down by
+confidential Send, and repay the same way. At the end, what is left of the float is
+retired in tranches by ConvertBack. It ran on Devnet on 2026-08-25, in 28
+validated facility transactions besides setting up the token (E-146).
+
+**Anyone can see** the size of the float, because converting it publishes the
+amount. They can see which suppliers enrolled, who drew and repaid, on which days,
+and how often. And they can see the size of every retirement tranche, because
+each ConvertBack publishes its own amount (F-24). My own walkthrough first said a
+ConvertBack published only *"the aggregate change"*. The validated transactions
+showed each tranche in plaintext.
+
+**Hidden from the public:** each supplier's limit, the size of each drawdown and
+repayment, and what each supplier still owes. The bank, as issuer, sees all of it.
+
+So it hides the shape of the book, not its size. An early version of the design
+claimed the facility *"shows nothing about which supplier drew how much"* (R-1).
+Which supplier drew, and when, is public.
+
+Two limits of that run. First, it read the ledger through a public Devnet node.
+The design requires a node on the same machine, and a local Devnet node never
+finished syncing on the hardware I had, so I accepted that as a named risk (E-148,
+E-151). Second, one test driver played the bank and every supplier and held every
+seed. The run shows that these transactions are well formed and that rippled
+accepts them. It does not show how custody would work.
+
+* * *
+
+## Reading the specification, and running it
+
+Several of the things above I learned only by running them:
+
+- That three different keys decrypt the same balance, through a change (E-58).
+- That the encryption of zero matches a value anyone can recompute (F-1).
+- That a balance spent to zero is not recognisable. My own observer page had
+  labelled every ciphertext that was not the fixed zero as *"Non-zero"*, and a
+  holder whose balance decrypted to 0 disproved it (E-211).
+- That a failing transaction is not simply rejected. A `tec` result is applied to
+  the ledger. The submission parameter `fail_hard` asks the node to discard it
+  instead. I ran both on Devnet with a plain Payment that fails with `tecNO_AUTH`:
+  the same signed bytes were applied without the flag, and discarded with it
+  (E-149).
+
+That last one matters more for confidential transactions than for plain ones,
+because a `tec` keeps the transaction's fields, ciphertexts included. If a signer
+reads a wrong destination key from a dishonest node, the amount is published
+encrypted to that key for good, even though the transaction fails. That case I
+read in rippled's source and did not run (F-23).
+
+Running is not a substitute for reading what others have already found. Several
+things I first recorded as findings turned out to be issues that Trail of Bits'
+April 2026 review had already found and Ripple had fixed.
+
+* * *
+
+## What the reviews caught
+
+Design decisions and fixes went through rounds of adversarial review. Reviewers
+were given deliberately different packets, so that their agreement would mean
+more than one reading copied three times. The repository keeps 61 numbered review
+records, including the ones that found me wrong. A few of the catches:
+
+- **A secret not wiped from memory, behind a comment explaining why it could not
+  be.** The comment said the secret's type belonged to an outside library. It was
+  the project's own type, and one search of its file showed it had no wiping at
+  all (E-200).
+- **A design claim that four reviewers independently ruled unsound.** I had
+  written that a read-only web tier *"moves no trust boundary"*. It added no
+  signing authority. But it re-served, to any local user, data the project
+  protects with file permissions (E-230).
+- **A release gate that passed a Content Security Policy every browser refused.**
+  The gate hashed inline scripts over the file's bytes. Browsers hash the text they
+  parse, which differs. Only loading the pages in a real browser showed it (E-334).
+- **Fixes that did not fix.** In one review's second round, five of the first
+  round's fixes had not discharged their findings. Only the reviewer that ran each
+  finding's own example against the fixed code found them (E-345).
+
+The lesson I keep relearning: fixing something and describing the fix are two
+acts that fail separately. A reviewer who reads my summary of a finding will tick
+the summary.
+
+* * *
+
+## Checks that catch a false sentence
+
+The working rule is that a claim needs its evidence before it is written. The
+claims register holds each established claim with what supports it, and twelve
+standing prohibitions, P-1 to P-12, on what may not be claimed at all: that XLS-96
+hides identities, that holders are private from the issuer, that it supports key
+rotation, any benchmark without its hardware and method, and any claim that a
+source does *not* say something without the search that would show otherwise.
+
+Prose drifts anyway, so some of it is enforced by checks that run in CI. One fails
+when a retracted phrase reappears without its correction. One fails when an
+observation filed or graded for upstream says a source does not say something,
+without the search recorded beside it. One keeps the register's derived indexes in
+step with it.
+
+They do not catch everything. The register keeps eight corrections, R-1 to R-8,
+each a sentence this project published and later found false. The last one, R-8,
+said every confidential transaction needs both of a holder's keys; a MergeInbox
+needs only the account key. It was on the public demo until a reviewer found it
+repeated in a diagram caption. And on 2026-10-18 the register still listed as open four
+filings that upstream had fixed in September (E-316). Nothing re-checked them until
+I surveyed every filing at source. That survey is now a gate on anything I publish
+about them, including this post.
+
+* * *
+
+## What went upstream
+
+Since 2026-08-26 this project has filed eleven issues in four XRPLF repositories.
+Their state on 2026-10-22, read at source (E-353):
+
+- **Four resolved in September.** Three issues against the XLS-0096 text were
+  resolved in the merged standard. The documentation's sentence calling the zero
+  value indistinguishable was corrected on the English page. The Japanese
+  translation was made from the text before the fix, and still carries it.
+- **The mpt-crypto build.** Its lockfile pinned an OpenSSL revision that the
+  documented package remote did not serve. Fixed on mpt-crypto's main branch on
+  2026-10-21, not yet in a release. I re-ran the check against the merged commit,
+  and it resolves.
+- **The fixed zero, from JavaScript.** mpt-crypto's WASM and npm packages did not
+  expose the function that computes the fixed encryption of zero, which is the
+  check an outside observer most needs. A maintainer agreed and a pull request is
+  approved and not merged. I have offered to write the JavaScript wrapper once it
+  is released.
+- **Three filed on 2026-10-18, against mpt-crypto, with no reply yet:** an
+  ambiguity in what the compact sigma paper's nonce input covers; a WASM build
+  script that fails outside its pinned toolchain; and a proof-size total in the
+  paper that assumes a ciphertext component is sent once, where rippled and
+  XLS-0096 send it per recipient.
+- **A question to XRPL-Standards**, whether a confidential balance is meant to stay
+  invisible to vault accounting, has had no reply in 57 days.
+- **A filing to rippled that listed only things done well** was closed without
+  comment the day it was filed. It fit neither of that repository's issue
+  templates. The project's filing rules now forbid a positives-only filing to a bug
+  tracker.
+
+I do not call any of these new, or unreported. Three reviews of this code exist.
+Trail of Bits' April 2026 report is the one I could read and check my findings
+against; a later revision of it could not be obtained. The Sherlock XRP Ledger
+Attackathon was a contest that covered Confidential Transfers, and its findings are
+not public. A Zellic scan of mpt-crypto is known to me only through three
+identifiers an upstream issue cites. Of the three, only Trail of Bits' April
+report could be checked.
+
+* * *
+
+## What it does not show
+
+- **No run against a local node.** Every Devnet read went to the public cluster
+  (E-151).
+- **Custody is accepted, not solved.** The issuer can erase or freeze the
+  facility's float. The Dedicated Account's key both moves the float and decrypts
+  every amount sent to or from it, so those two powers cannot be held apart
+  (E-266).
+- **The key derivation is unpublished.** It is specified in this repository only,
+  so a holder with their master seed but not this repository cannot reconstruct
+  their key. Treat it as lock-in until it is published.
+- **A hostile process running as the same user** can read the encryption secret
+  out of memory.
+
+* * *
+
+## Try it
+
+The demo is static pages built from one snapshot of Devnet. It signs nothing and
+holds no keys. It shows what an observer reads of four test accounts, including
+which balances are visibly zero; which encrypted copies the issuer can read,
+without publishing the figures; and what each kind of key can do. It does not show the facility, whose record is in the repository.
+
+To transact, you run the signer yourself, on your own machine. The README explains
+how to build it and run the local version of the site. It does not yet walk
+through creating a holder profile and funded Devnet accounts, which a transaction
+needs.
+
+The repository has the Rust signer, the TypeScript facility, the read-only web
+viewer, the claims register and the review records, under Apache-2.0.
+
+If something in this is wrong, please tell me, by an issue on the repository. The
+register has a section for corrections, and it has eight entries.
+
+* * *
+

# CLAUDE.md — W-CONF

Working instructions for coding sessions in this repository. This is the code-relevant subset of the project instructions. The publishing protocol is deliberately not here; it never applies inside a coding session.

## Hard rules

- **Devnet only.** No mainnet writes, at any phase, for any reason. ⚠ ~~The target network is the Confidential Devnet, not the general devnet.~~ **STRUCK 2026-09-01 — falsified by this project's own grade-A row on 2026-08-16 and carried in the HARD RULES for two weeks.** **No dedicated Confidential Devnet is needed or used, and whether one exists elsewhere was never searched** — the prerelease-documented one had a dead faucet, the canonical xrpl.org page names no dedicated network, and all three required amendments are enabled on **standard Devnet**, where everything this project has executed ran. ⚠ **`CLAIMS.md` E-26's own sentence says *"there is no dedicated Confidential Devnet"*, which is a corpus-wide negative its evidence cell does not support** — `amendments-2026-08-16.md:57` records the existence search as never run (P-12), `wss://s.devnet.rippletest.net:51233`, network_id 2. Everything this project has ever executed ran there. ⚠ **Found by a fresh reader of the README who could not open this file** and flagged the contradiction from the README's text alone (E-222). **The rule that survives is the first sentence**, and the target is standard Devnet.
- **Never assert amendment status from memory or a previous session.** Run `tools/check-amendments.ts` and date-stamp the answer.
- **Never claim more security than is delivered.** The standing prohibitions live in `CLAIMS.md`. Read them before writing a README, a comment, a commit message or a log line.
- **A named gap is a correct output; a substituted source is a corrupted one.** If a primary source is unreachable, record it in `CLAIMS.md` and move on. Do not backfill from secondary coverage and do not quietly drop the question.

## Review gates — scale to irreversibility

- Architecture, trust boundaries, cryptographic design, anything to be published: full adversarial rotation before implementation.
- Benchmark harnesses, measurement code, throwaway spikes: **build immediately**. The artifact self-verifies against test vectors and a review round adds nothing. `tools/check-amendments.ts` is in this category.

**Two rounds is the right number for a throwaway spike, and the second round reviews the FIXES.** Learned 2026-08-18 and worth not rediscovering. Round one found a defect the code had. Round two — run against the post-fix branch, because the fixes themselves had been seen by nobody — found a **false-pass mode in the regression test round one had written**, plus two sentences that overstated what the fixes established. Fixing something and describing the fix are separate acts with separate failure modes, and only a fresh reviewer catches the second kind. A third round would review the fixes to the fixes; that is where it stops paying.

⚠ **Apply a fix against the FINDING's own citation list, THEN GREP FOR THE PHRASE.** The first half was learned 2026-08-26 at the cost of a whole extra round; **the second half was learned 2026-08-27 by doing the first half correctly and still missing four sites** (E-168). `REVIEW-025c` recorded all eleven of its findings FIXED and `REVIEW-026` found four were not — every miss the same shape: *a fix applied to the instance the adjudicator was looking at, rather than to the phrase*. One sentence was corrected on the ed25519 test a leg cited and left standing on the identical secp256k1 sentence; another was fixed in a doc comment and left in **the section banner directly above it, inside the line range the leg had named**. ⚠ **A leg's list is line numbers. A corrected sentence is a string, and strings have copies.** `REVIEW-023c` said *"all seven upheld … every one is fixed"*; round two found that **three fixes had not reached sites the findings named by file and line** — two in the architecture document, one an entire `CLAIMS.md` row never touched. The adjudication had summarised *"nine live sentences"* and named six in prose; the leg's report listed all nine with paths. **A sweep re-derived from a summary is E-141's shape one layer up.** Tick the leg's list, not your own recollection of it.

⚠ **Do not commit your own self leg while a repo-access leg is reading the tree.** `REVIEW-022`'s lesson was *don't let files move under a leg*. The neighbouring one, learned 2026-08-26: **don't let your own answers appear in the tree a leg is reading.** Write the self leg to a scratchpad and commit it after the legs return. On the day this was learned the independence survived only because the Codex leg noticed the checkout was not the frozen commit and read the subject through `git show <frozen>:<path>` instead.

Record rejected reviewer claims with reasons so later sessions do not relitigate settled decisions.

## Preconditions before a build milestone

The spec exists, the architecture has passed adversarial review, and TASK ZERO is complete with its gaps recorded.

**Status 2026-08-18, revised late the same day.** GAP-1 and GAP-3 are closed. ADR-0001 §(a)'s threat-model question is **ruled** (issue #1: a hostile same-host process is in scope), which answers REVIEW-003b's MEDIUM and settles §(e)'s nonce half — implemented, reviewed twice, and executed on Devnet. The FFI blocker is closed (issue #2, path A, merged). **§(e)'s keygen half is now ruled too** (REVIEW-012, adjudicated REVIEW-012c), and the three long-missing primary documents are resolved — rippled 3.3.0 and the XLS-0096 text obtained, the Trail of Bits May 2026 revision recorded as an unobtainable gap (B-13).

**Status 2026-08-27 — B-16 is RULED, BUILT, EXECUTED and REVIEWED TWICE. `REVIEW-024` ruled it; `REVIEW-025` found eleven things wrong with the build, none of them the construction; `REVIEW-026` found that `REVIEW-025c` had OVERSTATED ITS OWN FIXES (E-168). All four of §7's conditions are met.** `REVIEW-024`, three independent legs (Gemini 9.0, Codex 8, self leg 7.5), **all ruling Option B**: the issue #1 ruling extends to the ed25519 signing nonce and the residual is **not** accepted. The RFC 8032 nonce prefix is hedged — 32 fresh CSPRNG bytes, tagged-hashed under a fixed DST and **XORed** over it, the same idiom site 1 uses — through `ed25519_dalek::hazmat::raw_sign` with the scalar, the public key, the challenge transcript and the signature equation untouched. **B-14 is now closed on both halves.**

**Status 2026-08-27, later the same day — B-21 is BUILT and REVIEWED TWICE, and building it proved B-19 WRONG (E-171).** `zeroize` is a direct `wconf-signer` dependency; `sha512_zeroizing`, `fresh_aux` and `OneShotAux` carry `Zeroizing`. 267 tests, three green runs, `make check-zeroize-bounds` is the falsifier — now **four parts**. `REVIEW-027` (three legs) and `REVIEW-028` (round two, the fixes). ⚠ **Eight leg-readings across three rounds, NOT ONE defect in the construction** — every finding was evidence, a gate, or a sentence. ~~⚠ **STILL OPEN: no Devnet run on the default signing path since B-21 landed**~~ — **EXECUTED at HEAD, `EF2018FA13AF7DCECD1D7562DE0BDF9A870688FAD6E4E564323B2AA1386FD336` (E-176).** `REVIEW-027` finding 8 is closed. ⚠ **The script now writes a receipt PER RUN and refuses to overwrite one from another commit** — E-169's mechanism, blocked rather than warned about.

**Status 2026-08-27, later still — B-22 is RULED, BUILT and REVIEWED TWICE, and round two found the build had NOT implemented its own ruling.** The key-derivation path wipes: `sha512half_zeroizing`, the ed25519 private key, both derivation closures, `derive_scalar`'s every rejected candidate, `root`/`intermediate`/`sum`, both heap seed decoders and their internals, and two `Copy`-source defects in `keygen.rs`. **268 tests at the time, three green runs, all six gates PASS. `make check-zeroize-bounds` is the falsifier — ~~now FIVE parts~~ five parts AT B-22; it is SIX as of B-23** (**274 tests as of B-24**), the fifth still pinning **thirteen named sites** — ⚠ **one was RETIRED by B-24, not lost: `Zeroizing(entropy)`'s `Copy`-source guard is gone because the producer now hands out a wiping type, so there is no bare source to guard** — with three controls that each run through the real detector. ⚠ **Corrected by the commit that falsified it** — a count in a status block is a claim about the CURRENT tree, and B-23 is the next commit after this sentence was written. `REVIEW-029` (the decision) and `REVIEW-030` (round two, the fixes, **two external legs** — which is what B-21's round two lacked).

**Five things B-22 established which a session will otherwise get wrong:**

- ⚠⚠ **WRAPPING A `Copy` TYPE IN A ZEROIZING WRAPPER DOES NOT WIPE THE SOURCE, AND THIS SESSION HIT IT FOUR TIMES.** `Zeroizing(entropy)` on a `[u8; 16]`, `Zeroizing(*sk.as_bytes())` on a `[u8; 32]`, and `Zeroizing::new(sha512half(&m))` — **the last of these was written INTO THE COMMIT THAT FIXED THE FIRST**, four hundred lines away, and found by both round-two legs (E-178, E-181). ⚠ **A wrapper around a `Copy` value copies; the original binding stays live.** The fix is either to bind and wipe the source, or — better — to build the value *into* the wiping buffer so no bare temporary ever exists.
- ⚠⚠ **THE RULING SAID THREE SCALARS WERE IN SCOPE, THE BUILD WIPED NONE OF THEM, AND A COMMENT CALLED THAT "THE CRATE'S BOUNDARY, NOT AN OMISSION".** Both round-two legs found it independently; a compile probe then showed `k256::NonZeroScalar` **and** `k256::Scalar` both implement `Zeroize`, so nothing had prevented it (E-181). ⚠ **This is precisely what `CLAUDE.md`'s two-round rule predicts — the construction was sound and the DESCRIPTION was hiding a real gap.** A session that reads its own fix report instead of the ruling will ship this.
- ⚠⚠ **A `Zeroizing` WRAPPED AROUND AN EXISTING BINDING HAS NO COMPILE-TIME FALSIFIER, AND THAT IS MEASURED (E-179).** Reverting `sha512half_zeroizing`'s **return type** breaks the build; reverting `Zeroizing::new(base58check_decode(..))` to the bare call gives **zero errors**, because `Zeroizing<T>` derefs to `T` and every use site compiles identically. ⚠ **Applying the revert machinery to those sites would have shipped a false pass of E-164's shape.** A source check is the honest instrument, and its guarantee is over a **NAMED SET** — a gate cannot prove no unlisted site exists.
- ⚠⚠ **A SOURCE-CHECK GATE THAT COUNTS A NEEDLE ANYWHERE FALSE-PASSES ON A COMMENTED-OUT LINE, and its controls must run through the REAL detector (E-182).** Part 5 shipped with both defects and both round-two legs found both: commenting out a production line still satisfied its needle, and the two controls re-ran the same count / checked an unrelated absence. ⚠ **Third instance in this repository of a gate built to catch false passes false-passing** (E-165, E-168). **Strip comments, and make every control call the same function the real check calls.**

**Three things step 7's opening established that a session will otherwise get wrong:**

- **`tesSUCCESS` was not accepted as the evidence, and that is the standard now.** All four of XLS-0096 §10.5's state changes were checked against ledger state before and after — public balance, `ConfidentialOutstandingAmount`, version, and the **decrypted** remainder. A `tesSUCCESS` alone does not distinguish a correct homomorphic subtraction from a lucky one.

**Status 2026-08-20 — architecture §6 step 6 is BUILT AND EXECUTED.** Real key generation and onboarding. **Issue #11 is discharged**: `lsfDisableMaster`, a regular key and a signer list each — on their own — flip the recommended key source to `standalone` and make the ruling's condition-2 warning mandatory, and the disclosures reach the holder **before the seed is asked for**. ⚠ **Issue #10 is NOT discharged and no code discharges it**: the derivation is specified in one repository document and is not a published standard, so a holder who has their seed and not this repository cannot reconstruct their key — which is the entire benefit the ruling trades a permanent decryption credential for. **Publishing an XLS informational draft is a Desktop-project decision, not a coding-session one.**

**Three things step 6 established that a session will otherwise get wrong:**

- **The ElGamal key now has TWO named sources**, and a profile declares which. `derived-from-master-seed` is the ruled construction and carries **no ElGamal secret in the profile at all**; `standalone` is the library's CSPRNG in `elgamal_sk`/`elgamal_pk` — which is what every profile before this milestone silently was. An absent `elgamal_key_source` reads as `standalone` and is **not** upgraded.
- **A registered key is not "unrecoverable", and saying so is a defect.** The protocol has no rotation and no recovery (P-10) — that is about **XLS-96**. A *derived* key is reconstructible from the master seed under the W-CONF derivation, which is the only thing deriving buys, and the confirmation said the opposite for one commit (E-125). ⚠ These are two sentences about two layers and merging them is how the banner also came to claim XLS-0096 governs XRPL account keys (E-126).
- **`from_parts` accepted a public key that was not `sk·G`.** Now `try_from_parts`, which recomputes it. The failure it allowed is the worst one this protocol offers: register a key nobody holds the secret for, encrypt every balance to it, and have every step succeed (E-120).

**ADR-0001 is `ACCEPTED` as of 2026-08-18** (`REVIEW-013c`). The last item — re-weigh Option 2 (browser WASM) on risk alone — was run: two independent legs, **both ruling Option 3**, both handed the strongest arguments against it. **Option 3 is confirmed on risk alone**, which is what rev 3 asked for and what the ADR previously could not do.

**Three things that rotation established, which a session will otherwise get wrong:**

- **The build-cost table was INVERTED, not merely stale.** Option 2 (browser WASM) is now the **cheapest** option — three published npm packages, no patching, no vendoring, no build step (E-53) — and Option 3 is the **most expensive**: a vendored C fork, an FFI binding, a Rust binary, OS-mediated IPC, a separate confirmation UI. **Option 3 was chosen anyway, on risk.** Do not repeat "Option 2 is expensive"; it is not.
- **An argument this project made three times was FALSE.** "Before the keygen ruling, an Option 2 page compromise did not touch spending authority" — false; the ADR's own table says Option 2's page can spend. The correct statement is that the keygen ruling **removes Option 2's escape hatch** (the browser can no longer delegate signing and hold only an ElGamal key, because the derivation input is the master seed) and **welds a rotatable exposure to an unrotatable one**. Use that form.
- ~~**`Accepted` unblocks architecture §6 step 7 and nothing else.** Steps 4 and 6 have their own gates, still shut.~~ **Both gates are now open.** Step 4 was built 2026-08-18 against A4–A9; step 6 was built and executed 2026-08-20. ⚠ **Step 7's own gates are not** — B-15 requires loopback, corroboration or a `tapFailHard` submitter, ADR-0002 is `Proposed`, and E-117's custody cost is unpriced.

**Rulings closed 2026-08-20** (see `docs/reviews/`): **B-14** — the transaction's ECDSA nonce is **hedged**, because the issue #1 ruling extends to it (`REVIEW-018`, E-109); ~~⚠ **secp256k1 only, ed25519 is B-16 and is the live path.**~~ **B-16 IS RULED TOO — 2026-08-27, `REVIEW-024`, E-158 — and NOT BUILT** (see the 2026-08-27 status block above). **B-15** — one ledger endpoint stands for this artifact **as a named risk acceptance** with a mandatory disclosure, and is a **gate on step 7** (`REVIEW-019`, E-110). **ADR-0002 round two** produced **revision 3**, which splits a Decision that asserted what the ADR reopened two sections later (`REVIEW-017c`, E-111) — **Decision A, native XLS-66 rejected, is settled and is what building proceeds on; Decision B, an XLS-65 `Vault` on the funding side, is open and gates the funding side only.**

⚠ **ADR-0002 is STILL `Proposed` — but on item 4 alone, which is research and not a decision.** ~~Its item 2 is a scope question that the ADR reserves for whoever owns scope~~ — **discharged 2026-08-20 in rev 4 (E-115), and NOT on the scope question.** Blocker 1 makes the hybrid a hard fork: `Vault` share tokens cannot be confidential, so it forces **native share accounting XOR confidential investor positions**, and the accounting is commodity while the confidentiality is the whole premise. ⚠ **The funder count therefore stops mattering** — one funder or twenty, all are confidential MPT holders and the architecture does not fork. ⚠ **Reversal condition:** if `lsfMPTCanHoldConfidentialBalance` ever becomes settable on a `Vault` share issuance, re-argue it. A leg argued the question dissolved on *structural* grounds instead; that was checked and rejected (E-112).

Do not treat these as one item.

**The architecture document** (`docs/architecture/ARCHITECTURE-2026-08-18.md`, **revision 6**) is explicitly provisional: it records what the rulings so far oblige and marks what is still open. ~~It does **not** license building application logic — that still waits on ADR-0001 reaching `Accepted`.~~ **ADR-0001 is now `Accepted`, so §6 step 7 is open.** §5 of that document is the authority on which gates remain shut — ~~`r`/`ρ` (A4–A9)~~ **built**, ~~onboarding that branches on ledger state (#11)~~ **built and executed 2026-08-20**, and **publication of the keygen derivation (#10), which is open and which no code discharges.**

**Status 2026-08-19 — §6 step 2 is built and executed.** The signer reads its own sequence number, confidential balance, `ConfidentialBalanceVersion`, registration state, the issuer and auditor keys and the destination's `HolderEncryptionKey` from a node, at one pinned validated index, and **re-reads before signing**. Nine fields left the holder profile, which now carries secrets and policy only and **refuses any of the nine by name**. Executed on Devnet (E-101).

**Two things that milestone established which a session will otherwise get wrong:**

- **A wrong ledger read is a CONFIDENTIALITY break, not a rejected transaction.** `tecBAD_PROOF` is a `tec`, and a `tec` is *applied to the ledger* — so a substituted destination key makes the signer publish the amount encrypted under the substituter's key, permanently. The signer does not submit, so it cannot set the `tapFailHard` that would prevent it. `CLAIMS.md` **F-23**, read at source, **not executed**. This is why TLS is mandatory for non-loopback endpoints and why B-15 exists.
- **`amount_search_to` now bounds the BALANCE as well as the confirmation.** The balance is decrypted from the ledger, so a balance above the bound is a balance the signer refuses to check an amount against. One earlier test's scenario became unreachable through `prepare` as a result and was moved rather than deleted (E-104).

**Step 2 was built before step 6 deliberately, and it was the right order.** Issue #11 requires detecting `lsfDisableMaster`, a regular key or a signer list — that *is* a ledger read. `AccountSecurity` reads all three today; **nothing branches on them yet**, and saying otherwise claims work that does not exist.

Remaining gaps are listed in `docs/task-zero/TASK-ZERO-2026-08-13.md` §0 and in the open GitHub issues.

Start with `GETTING-STARTED-CLAUDE-CODE.md`. The first three sessions are gap closure, not building.

**The holder signer is a separate Rust binary, not part of the web tree.** ADR-0001 puts proof generation and transaction signing in a daemon on the holder's machine; a browser page cannot invoke a local binary, so the two live side by side. Do not try to fold the signer into the TanStack/Elysia application.

⚠ **CORRECTED 2026-08-26. ADR-0001 rev 2's pasted-token design is **withdrawn**."* An origin allowlist constrains **pages**, not **processes**, any local process can forge an `Origin` header, and the issue #1 ruling puts a hostile same-host process in scope — so a value-shaped interface plus a leaked token is a **spend oracle**.

**What the signer actually speaks is a Unix domain socket** (`signer/src/ipc.rs`), chosen because architecture §3 item 4 prefers OS-mediated IPC. Grants are scoped, short-lived and **bound to the connection**; closing the connection revokes them.

⚠ **The consequence for the web tier, and it is the first thing architecture §6 step 8 has to answer: a browser page CANNOT REACH THE SIGNER AT ALL.** `ipc.rs`: *"A browser page cannot connect at all. No web API opens a Unix socket."* That is the point — it closes the XSS-to-spend-oracle path by construction rather than by a header check. **Any step-8 design that gets a browser signing confidential transactions is a trust-boundary change and needs a full adversarial rotation before implementation, not after.**

## Keys

~~Never write ElGamal keygen code before the Cryptography Reviewer has ruled on ADR-0001 §(e).~~ **Ruled 2026-08-18, implemented and executed 2026-08-20.** The construction lives in `docs/reviews/REVIEW-012-RULING-keygen-2026-08-18.md` and **only** there — do not paraphrase it into the ADR or the architecture document. `signer/src/keygen.rs` is an *implementation* of that prose and says so; where the two disagree, the ruling wins. Derivation from the XRPL master seed is upheld, with five conditions.

**Three things about that ruling that a coding session will otherwise get wrong:**

- **Its reduction is TOTAL and has no abort path**, unlike the sigma-nonce and `r`/`ρ` rulings, which both say *abort on zero, never retry*. That is correct there, where the input is fresh entropy and an abort costs one transaction. Keygen's input is a **fixed seed**, so an abort would be permanent — that holder could never participate. Do not "fix" it back.
- **Condition 2 is not cosmetic.** Onboarding must disclose that the master seed becomes a permanent decryption credential, and the signer must **warn** when the account carries `lsfDisableMaster`, a regular key or a signer list (E-69). For those holders the master seed is not spending authority, and §(e)'s argument for derivation does not hold.
- **The registration PoK must always be passed a non-NULL `context_id`.** The library accepts NULL and then emits an account-unbound, replayable proof (F-19). rippled cannot reach that path; our signer can.

~~When keygen is written, validate it against~~ **Done 2026-08-20.** mpt-crypto's own tests — `test_pok_sk`, `test_elgamal`, `test_elgamal_verify` — are C programs over **random** keys, so `signer/tests/keygen_interop.rs` drives their *properties* with a derived key. **Necessary, not sufficient:** a constant `sk_A = 1` passes all three, and **that claim is now itself a test** — `a_constant_sk_of_one_passes_every_upstream_check` runs it and asserts they pass, which is what makes the KAT load-bearing rather than decorative. The derivation's own KAT is `tools/spike-keygen-2026-08-18/t-keygen-construction.ts` and `signer/tests/keygen_kat.rs`.

### 1. After the LinkedIn post only

* **Is confidential transfer possible on the XRP Ledger, and with what limits?**  
  Yes, but currently only on the Devnet test network under the proposed XLS-96 amendment, not on Mainnet or Testnet. It provides narrow privacy: it encrypts holder balances and peer-to-peer transfer amounts, but leaves counterparties, transaction timing, conversion amounts into/out of confidential form, certain zero balances, and total float completely public, while the issuer can always see every balance and no key recovery exists.
* **Would you click through, and why or why not?**  
  Yes. In commercial finance, confidentiality is a prerequisite for moving real-world assets onto public ledgers. The post is compelling because it avoids crypto marketing hype, immediately establishes strict limits on privacy, admits lack of audit/production readiness, and cites concrete upstream technical contributions.
* **What do you think the author is claiming to have done?**  
  The author claims to have implemented the core ledger logic of a receivables financing facility on Devnet using XLS-96, empirically tested what an external observer can and cannot see on-ledger, uncovered discrepancies between the specification/documentation and live network behavior, and submitted 11 bug reports and fixes upstream to XRPLF repositories.

---

### 2. After the blog post

* **What is hidden and what is public:**  
  *Hidden:* Individual account balances and the exact amounts transferred during a confidential `Send`. In the receivables facility, each supplier's credit limit, the size of individual drawdowns and repayments, and each supplier’s outstanding balance remain hidden.  
  *Public:* The transaction graph (sender, receiver, timestamp, and frequency), all amounts converted into or out of confidential form (`Convert` and `ConvertBack`), total token supply, total confidential pool size, specific zero balances (newly initialized accounts, freshly emptied inboxes, and clawed-back balances), the total facility float, and each tranche retirement amount.
* **Who can read a balance and who can spend it:**  
  *Read:* The balance holder, the token issuer (who holds an unavoidable ElGamal decryption copy for every account), and an optional single designated auditor if configured at token creation.  
  *Spend:* Exclusively the possessor of the holder’s encryption secret (required to construct the zero-knowledge proofs). The issuer cannot spend a holder's balance, but can destroy it via clawback or freeze it via ledger flags if permitted.
* **What happens if a key is lost:**  
  The funds are permanently lost and unspendable. XLS-96 lacks key rotation or recovery mechanisms, and the proposed XLS-99 standard is not yet supported on any live network. The only recourse is an issuer clawback, which permanently destroys the tokens without returning them.
* **What the receivables facility example shows and does not show:**  
  *Shows:* That the sequential lifecycle of an on-ledger confidential credit facility (float funding, supplier drawdowns, repayments, and tranche retirements) can be constructed and validated by `rippled` on Devnet, proving that macro cash flows can be published while hiding micro-level counterparty balances.  
  *Does not show:* How real-world key custody and multi-party separation would work (a single test script acted as bank and all suppliers holding all seeds), whether it runs against a private local node (it relied on a public Devnet cluster), or how to separate viewing rights from spending rights on the Dedicated Account.
* **What went upstream and what happened to it:**  
  The author submitted 11 issues across four XRPLF repositories:
  * 4 resolved in September (spec corrections incorporated into final XLS-96; English documentation corrected regarding zero-balance indistinguishability).
  * 1 build fix (`mpt-crypto` OpenSSL dependency pinning) merged to main on 2026-10-21, awaiting release.
  * 1 pull request approved to expose the zero-encryption calculation in JavaScript/WASM, awaiting merge.
  * 3 issues filed on 2026-10-18 against `mpt-crypto` (nonce scope ambiguity, toolchain build failure, proof size calculation discrepancy) awaiting responses.
  * 1 architectural question to XRPL-Standards regarding vault accounting, unanswered after 57 days.
  * 1 "positives-only" issue closed immediately by `rippled` maintainers for failing to use bug report templates.
* **What the three reviews of the code are:**  
  Here the post fails the reader through ambiguous phrasing. Under the heading *"What went upstream"*, the post states *"Three reviews of this code exist"*, referring to external audits of *upstream/XRPLF code*: (1) Trail of Bits' April 2026 report, (2) the Sherlock XRP Ledger Attackathon, and (3) a Zellic scan of `mpt-crypto`. Conversely, reviews of the author’s *own* project code were not traditional audits at all; they were automated review rounds conducted by other AI models (Codex, Gemini) and separate Claude sessions across 61 internal review records.

### 3. Where you got lost

* **Terms used before explained, or never explained:**
  * `"Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs, XLS-33) are one of its token types."`  
    *MPT* is never explained. A reader unfamiliar with XRPL does not know what an MPT is, what properties it has, or how it differs from standard issued currencies.
  * `"Each confidential balance is an ElGamal ciphertext."`  
    *ElGamal ciphertext* is introduced without explaining that ElGamal is an asymmetric encryption scheme that supports public-key encryption and dual-recipient encryption (which explains why the issuer can also decrypt it).
  * `"Tess Dore and Murat Cenk's compact sigma protocol"` / `"The compact sigma protocol behind its send proof..."`  
    *Sigma protocol* is never defined or explained as the underlying zero-knowledge proof technique.
  * `"- MergeInbox moves what a holder has received into the balance they can spend."`  
    The concept of an "inbox" is never introduced before this bullet. A reader does not know why incoming funds land in a distinct inbox rather than directly into the spendable balance, nor why a separate transaction is required to merge them.
  * `"If the token allows clawback, the issuer can destroy it..."`  
    *Clawback* is used without clarifying that it is an XRPL-specific token feature allowing issuers to unilaterally seize or revoke balances.
  * `"A Dedicated Account, an ordinary XRPL account, holds the float..."`  
    Capitalized as if *Dedicated Account* is an XRPL protocol primitive or smart contract type, rather than merely an operational convention chosen by the author.
  * `"A tec result is applied to the ledger. ... a plain Payment that fails with tecNO_AUTH:"`  
    *tec* and *tecNO_AUTH* are completely unexplained. A newcomer has no idea that `tec` represents an XRPL transaction engine error code that still consumes fees and mutates ledger state.
  * `"...whether a confidential balance is meant to stay invisible to vault accounting..."`  
    *Vault accounting* is introduced out of nowhere with zero context as to what vaults are on the XRPL.

* **Sentences read twice:**
  * `"Read on 2026-10-22 at 03:25 UTC, its amendment, ConfidentialTransfer, was enabled on Devnet, and supported but not enabled on Mainnet and Testnet."`  
    The opening participle "Read on..." reads awkwardly like an instruction or truncated sentence before you realize it means "As observed on...".
  * `"Three reviews of this code exist. Trail of Bits' April 2026 report is the one I could read and check my findings against; a later revision of it could not be obtained."`  
    The antecedent of "this code" is thoroughly confusing. Having just discussed the author's own project and upstream repositories, it sounds like Trail of Bits reviewed the author's project, when it actually reviewed upstream `mpt-crypto`.
  * `"One fails when an observation filed or graded for upstream says a source does not say something, without the search recorded beside it."`  
    The layered double-negatives and internal jargon ("graded for upstream", "says a source does not say something") require multiple passes to parse.

* **Anything in the wrong order:**
  * **Placement of upstream audit mentions:** The paragraph discussing the Trail of Bits, Sherlock, and Zellic reviews is buried at the end of *"What went upstream"*. It belongs either in an introductory background section on XLS-96 or clearly segregated from the section *"What the reviews caught"*, which discussed AI reviews of the author's code.
  * **Error handling / `tec` failure risks:** The critical privacy revelation—that failed `tec` transactions permanently publish ciphertexts encrypted to bad recipient keys on-ledger—is placed under *"Reading the specification, and running it"* rather than under *"What it hides, and what it does not"*.

### 4. Where it reads stronger than it should

* **Misleading impressions of security, audits, and privacy:**
  * *"Three reviews of this code exist. Trail of Bits' April 2026 report is the one I could read and check my findings against..."*  
    Calling upstream libraries *"this code"* strongly implies that the author's codebase has been audited by Trail of Bits, Sherlock, and Zellic.
  * *"Design decisions and fixes went through rounds of adversarial review."*  
    The term *"adversarial review"* strongly connotes formal third-party security audits, red-teaming, or penetration testing, rather than automated prompting across LLM sessions (Claude, Codex, Gemini).
  * *"It hides the shape of the book, not its size."*  
    In credit facilities, the "shape of the book" includes the network graph: who the borrower counterparties are, when they borrow, and borrowing frequency. Because all counterparties, transaction timestamps, and activity patterns are public, the facility only hides the *values/amounts*, not the structural shape of borrowing activity.

  * **What "shape of the book" means:**  
    *Sentence 1:* `It hides the shape of the book, not its size.`  
    *Sentence 2:* `Which supplier drew, and when, is public.` (reinforced by: `They can see which suppliers enrolled, who drew and repaid, on which days, and how often.`)
  * **Web tier safety and keys:**  
    *Sentence 1:* `The demo is static pages built from one snapshot of Devnet. It signs nothing and holds no keys.`  
    *Sentence 2:* `I had written that a read-only web tier "moves no trust boundary". It added no signing authority. But it re-served, to any local user, data the project protects with file permissions (E-230).` (and: `A hostile process running as the same user can read the encryption secret out of memory.`)

FIXED BLOG
     1	# Amounts, not relationships: what confidential transfers on the XRP Ledger hide
     2	
     3	*Status, before anything else: this is a research project on the XRP Ledger's
     4	Devnet test network. It is not audited, not production-ready, and not safe to put
     5	value behind. Its signer refuses every network but Devnet.*
     6	
     7	Can a token move confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, under a standard called
     8	XLS-96, and today only on Devnet. When I checked on 2026-10-22 at 03:25 UTC, its
     9	amendment, `ConfidentialTransfer`, was enabled on Devnet, and supported but not
    10	enabled on Mainnet and Testnet. That reading goes stale. The repository has a
    11	script that takes a fresh one.
    12	
    13	What XLS-96 hides is narrower than the word *confidential* suggests. It hides
    14	balances, and the amounts of transfers between confidential balances. It does not
    15	hide who pays whom, when, or how often. It does not hide amounts entering or
    16	leaving confidential form. And it hides nothing from the token's issuer.
    17	
    18	Since mid-August I have been building an application on it to find out exactly
    19	where that line falls, by running transactions rather than by reading the
    20	specification. This post is what I found, what the reviews of my own work caught,
    21	and what went back upstream. The project is called W-CONF. The code and its claims
    22	register are public at
    23	[github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions](https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions),
    24	and a read-only demo is at
    25	[xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app](https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app).
    26	
    27	Ids such as *E-58* in this post are rows in the project's claims register,
    28	[`CLAIMS.md`](https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions/blob/main/CLAIMS.md).
    29	Each row says what supports it. Where this post and a row disagree, the row wins.
    30	
    31	* * *
    32	
    33	## What XLS-96 is, briefly
    34	
    35	The XRP Ledger is public: anyone can read every account and every transaction.
    36	Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs, XLS-33) are one of its token types: an account issues
    37	a token, and other accounts hold it. XLS-96, Confidential Transfers for MPTs, lets
    38	a holder keep an MPT balance encrypted on that public ledger.
    39	
    40	Each confidential balance is an ElGamal ciphertext, a public-key encryption of the
    41	amount. A holder registers their own encryption key when they opt in. The ledger
    42	still has to stop anyone spending more than they hold, so every transaction that
    43	spends from a confidential balance carries zero-knowledge proofs, which validators
    44	check without learning the amount.
    45	
    46	A position moves through four transactions:
    47	
    48	- **Convert** moves tokens from a public balance into the holder's confidential
    49	  inbox. The amount is published.
    50	- **Send** moves an amount from one confidential balance into another holder's
    51	  inbox. The amount is hidden. The sender and receiver are not.
    52	- **MergeInbox** moves the inbox into the balance the holder can spend. Tokens in
    53	  the inbox cannot be sent until they are merged.
    54	- **ConvertBack** moves tokens back to a public balance. The amount is published.
    55	
    56	Only Send hides an amount.
    57	
    58	The specification, XLS-0096, is the work of Murat Cenk, Aanchal Malhotra, Ayo
    59	Akinyele, Peter Chen, Shawn Xie and Yinyi Qian, and has been `Final` since
    60	2026-09-03 (E-1). The compact sigma protocol, the zero-knowledge proof behind a
    61	Send, is the work of Tess Dore and Murat Cenk at RippleX Research. The reference
    62	cryptography is [`XRPLF/mpt-crypto`](https://github.com/XRPLF/mpt-crypto). This
    63	project builds on their work and claims none of it.
    64	
    65	Upstream's code has had three outside reviews. None of them reviewed this
    66	project, which has had no outside audit. Trail of Bits reviewed upstream's
    67	Confidential Transfer implementation in April 2026; that report is the one I could
    68	read and check my findings against, and a later revision of it could not be
    69	obtained. The Sherlock XRP Ledger Attackathon was a contest that covered
    70	Confidential Transfers, and its findings are not public. A Zellic scan of
    71	mpt-crypto is known to me only through three identifiers an upstream issue cites.
    72	Of the three, only Trail of Bits' April report could be checked.
    73	
    74	* * *
    75	
    76	## What it hides, and what it does not
    77	
    78	**Hidden from the public:** each holder's balance, and the amount of each Send.
    79	
    80	**Public, always:**
    81	
    82	- The sender and receiver of every transfer, and when it happened, so how often
    83	  anyone transacts (P-4, P-11).
    84	- Every amount converted in or out, each one separately.
    85	- The token's total supply, and the total held in confidential form.
    86	- That a balance is exactly zero, in three cases, below.
    87	
    88	**Who can read every balance:** the issuer, always. XLS-96 keeps a second copy of
    89	each confidential balance, encrypted to the issuer's key, and no setting turns it
    90	off (P-9). An auditor can read them too, if the token names one, and only one is
    91	supported (E-11). I ran this rather than inferring it. The holder, the issuer and
    92	the auditor each decrypted the same balance, 500, and each read 475 after a
    93	25-unit Send (E-58).
    94	
    95	**Who can spend:** only whoever holds the holder's encryption secret, because a
    96	Send's proof cannot be made without it (E-33). Where that secret is derived from
    97	the account's master seed, as this project derives it, whoever holds the seed
    98	holds the secret too. The issuer cannot spend a holder's balance. If the token
    99	allows clawback, a setting that lets an issuer take tokens back, the issuer can
   100	destroy a confidential balance, crediting no one, and this project's tokens allow
   101	clawback (E-12). Unless the token's flags were made unchangeable when it was
   102	created, the issuer can also turn on locking later and freeze balances. That
   103	second power I read in rippled's source and did not run (E-290).
   104	
   105	**Zero is sometimes visible.** XLS-96 writes a fixed encryption of zero, which
   106	anyone can recompute from public inputs, in three places: a new confidential
   107	balance, an inbox that a MergeInbox has just emptied, and a position clawed back.
   108	So enrolment is publicly visible. The English documentation said this value could
   109	not be told apart from other ciphertexts. I recomputed it from public inputs and
   110	matched it byte for byte against live Devnet state (F-1, E-59), reported it, and
   111	the English page was corrected in September. A balance spent down to zero holds a
   112	randomised encryption of zero, and is not recognisable (E-211).
   113	
   114	**The public numbers bound the hidden ones.** If a holder converts in 500, receives
   115	nothing, and converts back 400, anyone can work out that the other 100 is either
   116	still held or has left by confidential Send. No key is needed. I first wrote that
   117	the 100 *"left by transfer"*. That overstated what an observer learns, and it is
   118	recorded as a correction (R-7).
   119	
   120	* * *
   121	
   122	## No rotation, no recovery
   123	
   124	A registered key can never be changed (E-9). XLS-96 has no key rotation and no key
   125	recovery (P-10). If a holder loses their key, and any seed it could be re-derived
   126	from, the balance cannot be spent. The only remedy is an issuer clawback, which
   127	destroys the balance.
   128	
   129	A draft standard, XLS-99, by Aanchal Malhotra and Yinyi Qian, proposes rotation for
   130	holder, issuer and auditor keys, and recovery from key loss. On 2026-10-22,
   131	rippled's development branch and its release candidate `3.5.0-rc1` declared its
   132	amendment as not supported, and Mainnet, Testnet and Devnet did not know it (E-353).
   133	So there is no rotation or recovery in XLS-96, or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet,
   134	today.
   135	
   136	* * *
   137	
   138	## The example: a confidential receivables facility
   139	
   140	To test the standard against something with stakes, I built the core of a
   141	receivables facility. A bank pays a large buyer's suppliers early, against their
   142	invoices. How much a supplier draws says a lot about its cash position, so these
   143	amounts are commercially sensitive.
   144	
   145	The bank issues a token. An ordinary XRPL account, which this project calls the
   146	Dedicated Account, holds the float and converts it into confidential form once.
   147	Suppliers enrol, draw down by confidential Send, and repay the same way. At the
   148	end, what is left of the float is retired in tranches by ConvertBack. It ran on
   149	Devnet on 2026-08-25, in 28 validated facility transactions besides setting up the
   150	token (E-146).
   151	
   152	**Anyone can see** the size of the float, because converting it publishes the
   153	amount. They can see which suppliers enrolled, who drew and repaid, on which days,
   154	and how often. And they can see the size of every retirement tranche, because
   155	each ConvertBack publishes its own amount (F-24). My own walkthrough first said a
   156	ConvertBack published only *"the aggregate change"*. The validated transactions
   157	showed each tranche in plaintext.
   158	
   159	**Hidden from the public:** each supplier's limit, the size of each drawdown and
   160	repayment, and what each supplier still owes. The bank, as issuer, sees all of it.
   161	
   162	So it hides how much each supplier draws and owes. It does not hide who borrows,
   163	when, how often, or the size of the whole. An early version of the design claimed
   164	the facility *"shows nothing about which supplier drew how much"* (R-1). Which
   165	supplier drew, and when, is public.
   166	
   167	Two limits of that run. First, it read the ledger through a public Devnet node.
   168	The design requires a node on the same machine, and a local Devnet node never
   169	finished syncing on the hardware I had, so I accepted that as a named risk (E-148,
   170	E-151). Second, one test driver played the bank and every supplier and held every
   171	seed. The run shows that these transactions are well formed and that rippled
   172	accepts them. It does not show how custody would work.
   173	
   174	* * *
   175	
   176	## Reading the specification, and running it
   177	
   178	Several of the things above I learned only by running them:
   179	
   180	- That three different keys decrypt the same balance, through a change (E-58).
   181	- That the encryption of zero matches a value anyone can recompute (F-1).
   182	- That a balance spent to zero is not recognisable. My own observer page had
   183	  labelled every ciphertext that was not the fixed zero as *"Non-zero"*, and a
   184	  holder whose balance decrypted to 0 disproved it (E-211).
   185	- That a failing transaction is not simply rejected. A `tec` result, one class of
   186	  XRPL failure code, is still applied to the ledger and consumes the account's
   187	  sequence number. The submission parameter `fail_hard` asks the node to discard
   188	  it instead. I ran both on Devnet with a plain Payment that fails with `tecNO_AUTH`:
   189	  the same signed bytes were applied without the flag, and discarded with it
   190	  (E-149).
   191	
   192	That last one matters more for confidential transactions than for plain ones,
   193	because a `tec` keeps the transaction's fields, ciphertexts included. If a signer
   194	reads a wrong destination key from a dishonest node, the amount is published
   195	encrypted to that key for good, even though the transaction fails. That case I
   196	read in rippled's source and did not run (F-23).
   197	
   198	Running is not a substitute for reading what others have already found. Several
   199	things I first recorded as findings turned out to be issues that Trail of Bits'
   200	April 2026 review had already found and Ripple had fixed.
   201	
   202	* * *
   203	
   204	## What the reviews caught
   205	
   206	Design decisions and fixes went through rounds of adversarial review. These were
   207	the project's own review rounds, not outside audits. Each round gave its
   208	reviewers deliberately different packets, so that their agreement would mean more
   209	than one reading copied three times. The repository keeps 61 numbered review records,
   210	including the ones that found me wrong. A few of the catches:
   211	
   212	- **A secret not wiped from memory, behind a comment explaining why it could not
   213	  be.** The comment said the secret's type belonged to an outside library. It was
   214	  the project's own type, and one search of its file showed it had no wiping at
   215	  all (E-200).
   216	- **A design claim that four reviewers independently ruled unsound.** I had
   217	  written that the project's local read-only web viewer *"moves no trust
   218	  boundary"*. It added no signing authority. But it re-served, to any local user,
   219	  data the project protects with file permissions (E-230). That was the viewer
   220	  that runs on the holder's machine, before the hosted demo existed; the demo
   221	  serves only static files.
   222	- **A release gate that passed a Content Security Policy every browser refused.**
   223	  The gate hashed inline scripts over the file's bytes. Browsers hash the text they
   224	  parse, which differs. Only loading the pages in a real browser showed it (E-334).
   225	- **Fixes that did not fix.** In one review's second round, five of the first
   226	  round's fixes had not discharged their findings. Only the reviewer that ran each
   227	  finding's own example against the fixed code found them (E-345).
   228	
   229	The lesson I keep relearning: fixing something and describing the fix are two
   230	acts that fail separately. A reviewer who reads my summary of a finding will tick
   231	the summary.
   232	
   233	* * *
   234	
   235	## Checks that catch a false sentence
   236	
   237	The working rule is that a claim needs its evidence before it is written. The
   238	claims register holds each established claim with what supports it, and twelve
   239	standing prohibitions, P-1 to P-12, on what may not be claimed at all: that XLS-96
   240	hides identities, that holders are private from the issuer, that it supports key
   241	rotation, any benchmark without its hardware and method, and any claim that a
   242	source does *not* say something without the search that would show otherwise.
   243	
   244	Prose drifts anyway, so some of it is enforced by checks that run in CI. One fails
   245	when a retracted phrase reappears without its correction. One fails when a note
   246	meant for upstream says something is missing from a source and does not record the
   247	search that found it missing. One keeps the register's derived indexes in step
   248	with it.
   249	
   250	They do not catch everything. The register keeps eight correction records, R-1 to
   251	R-8. Most withdraw or narrow something this project claimed; one records a
   252	retraction that was itself reversed. The last one, R-8, said every confidential
   253	transaction needs both of a holder's keys; a MergeInbox needs only the account
   254	key. It was on the public demo until a reviewer found it repeated in a diagram
   255	caption. And on 2026-10-18 the register still listed as open four filings that
   256	upstream had fixed in September (E-316). Nothing re-checked them until
   257	I surveyed every filing at source. That survey is now a gate on anything I publish
   258	about them, including this post.
   259	
   260	* * *
   261	
   262	## What went upstream
   263	
   264	Since 2026-08-26 this project has filed eleven issues in four XRPLF repositories.
   265	Their state on 2026-10-22, read at source (E-353):
   266	
   267	- **Four resolved in September.** Three issues against the XLS-0096 text were
   268	  resolved in the merged standard. The documentation's sentence calling the zero
   269	  value indistinguishable was corrected on the English page. The Japanese
   270	  translation was made from the text before the fix, and still carries it.
   271	- **The mpt-crypto build.** Its lockfile pinned an OpenSSL revision that the
   272	  documented package remote did not serve. Fixed on mpt-crypto's main branch on
   273	  2026-10-21, not yet in a release. I re-ran the check against the merged commit,
   274	  and it resolves.
   275	- **The fixed zero, from JavaScript.** mpt-crypto's WASM and npm packages did not
   276	  expose the function that computes the fixed encryption of zero, which is the
   277	  check an outside observer most needs. A maintainer agreed and a pull request is
   278	  approved and not merged. I have offered to write the JavaScript wrapper once it
   279	  is released.
   280	- **Three filed on 2026-10-18, against mpt-crypto, with no reply yet:** an
   281	  ambiguity in what the compact sigma paper's nonce input covers; a WASM build
   282	  script that fails outside its pinned toolchain; and a proof-size total in the
   283	  paper that assumes a ciphertext component is sent once, where rippled and
   284	  XLS-0096 send it per recipient.
   285	- **A question to XRPL-Standards**, whether a confidential balance is meant to stay
   286	  invisible to the accounting of the ledger's vaults (XLS-65), has had no reply in
   287	  57 days.
   288	- **A filing to rippled that listed only things done well** was closed without
   289	  comment the day it was filed, so its reason is not known. It also fit neither of
   290	  that repository's two issue templates, and the project's filing rules now forbid
   291	  a positives-only filing to a bug tracker.
   292	
   293	I do not call any of these new, or unreported. Of the three outside reviews of
   294	upstream's code, I could check my findings against one.
   295	
   296	* * *
   297	
   298	## What it does not show
   299	
   300	- **No run against a local node.** Every Devnet read went to the public cluster
   301	  (E-151).
   302	- **Custody is accepted, not solved.** The issuer can erase or freeze the
   303	  facility's float. The Dedicated Account's key both moves the float and decrypts
   304	  every amount sent to or from it, so those two powers cannot be held apart
   305	  (E-266).
   306	- **The key derivation is unpublished.** It is specified in this repository only,
   307	  so a holder with their master seed but not this repository cannot reconstruct
   308	  their key. Treat it as lock-in until it is published.
   309	- **A hostile process running as the same user** can read the encryption secret
   310	  out of memory.
   311	
   312	* * *
   313	
   314	## Try it
   315	
   316	The demo is static pages built from one snapshot of Devnet. It signs nothing and
   317	holds no keys. It shows what an observer reads of four test accounts, including
   318	which balances are visibly zero; which encrypted copies the issuer can read,
   319	without publishing the figures; and what each kind of key can do. It does not show
   320	the facility, whose record is in the repository.
   321	
   322	To transact, you run the signer yourself, on your own machine. The README explains
   323	how to build it and run the local version of the site. It does not yet walk
   324	through creating a holder profile and funded Devnet accounts, which a transaction
   325	needs.
   326	
   327	The repository has the Rust signer, the TypeScript facility, the read-only web
   328	viewer, the claims register and the review records, under Apache-2.0.
   329	
   330	If something in this is wrong, please tell me, by an issue on the repository. The
   331	register has a section for corrections, and it has eight entries.
   332

     6	---
     7	
     8	Is confidential transfer possible on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on Devnet only. XLS-96 is a final standard, and when I checked on 2026-10-22 its amendment, ConfidentialTransfer, was enabled on Devnet and not on Mainnet or Testnet.
     9	
    10	It hides less than the word suggests. I built the core of a receivables facility on it and ran it on Devnet to find out exactly what an outside observer sees.
    11	
    12	Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each transfer between confidential balances.
    13	
    14	Public: who pays whom, when, and how often. Every amount converted into or out of confidential form. Some zero balances, which anyone can recognise.
    15	
    16	The issuer can read every balance, always. No setting turns that off.
    17	
    18	There is no key rotation or recovery in XLS-96, or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet today. A draft standard, XLS-99, proposes both.
    19	
    20	In the facility, that means the size of the float, which suppliers drew on which days, and every retirement tranche are public. Each supplier's limit, the size of each drawdown and what each supplier owes are not. It hides how much, not who or when.
    21	
    22	Along the way I filed eleven issues with XRPLF repositories. Upstream resolved four in September and fixed a fifth on 2026-10-21, not yet in a release. The rest are open, waiting, or closed without comment. The write-up describes each one, and names the three outside reviews of upstream's code.
    23	
    24	This is a research project on a test network. It is not audited, and not production-ready.
    25	
    26	The write-up: <BLOG-URL>
    27	A read-only demo: https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app
    28	The code and the claims register: https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions
    29	
    30	XLS-96 is the work of Murat Cenk, Aanchal Malhotra, Ayo Akinyele, Peter Chen, Shawn Xie and Yinyi Qian, with Tess Dore and Murat Cenk's compact sigma protocol.

    41	 *    TRUE sentence wrapped to contain a phrase is now rejected, which is the
    42	 *    loud direction.

    60	 * every third line — so that window forgives almost anything. **Over-forgiving
    61	 * is the unsafe direction for a gate that enforces an absence** (E-203's
    62	 * two-consumers lesson), so each entry names the row that retracted it.
