   205	const EXEMPT_DIRS = ["docs/reviews/", "node_modules", "/.git/", "/target/", "/dist/"];
   206	/** ⚠ This file necessarily contains every phrase. See "What it does NOT say" 4. */
   207	const EXEMPT_FILES = ["tools/check-disclosure-phrases.ts"];
   208	/**
   209	 * ⚠⚠ **`.tsx` WAS MISSING, SO THIS GATE COULD NOT SEE THE RENDERED UI AT ALL —
   210	 * `REVIEW-037` F1, `CLAIMS.md` E-234.** The web tier's pages are `.tsx`, and a
   211	 * page is **the largest disclosure surface this project has built**: it is the
   212	 * one place a claim reaches a human who cannot read the source. The gate that
   213	 * exists to stop a retracted claim being asserted was blind to every one of
   214	 * them. ⚠ **`.jsx` is included for the same reason, though the tier has none.**
   215	 */
   216	const LIVE_EXT = [".md", ".rs", ".ts", ".tsx", ".jsx", ".py", ".toml", ".json"];
   217	/** Lines either side of a hit that are searched for a marker. */
   218	const WINDOW = 6;
   219	
   220	/**
   221	 * ⚠ **One of these MUST be in the window before any hit is forgiven** — E-238.
   222	 * A phrase's own markers say *which* retraction; these say *that* it is one.
   223	 */
   224	const RETRACTION_TOKENS = ["~~", "STRUCK", "RETRACTED", "SUPERSEDED", "no longer"];
   225	
   226	export interface Hit {
   227	  file: string;
   228	  line: number;
   229	  phrase: string;
   230	  why: string;
   231	}
   232	
   233	function liveFiles(dir = "."): string[] {
   234	  const out: string[] = [];
   235	  for (const name of readdirSync(dir)) {
   236	    const p = join(dir, name);
   237	    if (EXEMPT_DIRS.some((d) => (p + "/").includes(d.replace(/^\.?\//, "")))) continue;
   238	    let st;
   239	    try { st = statSync(p); } catch { continue; }
   240	    if (st.isDirectory()) { out.push(...liveFiles(p)); continue; }
   241	    if (!LIVE_EXT.some((e) => p.endsWith(e))) continue;
   242	    if (EXEMPT_FILES.some((f) => p.endsWith(f))) continue;
   243	    out.push(p);
   244	  }
   245	  return out;
   246	}
   247	
   248	/**
   249	 * The text as a reader would see it, flattened: on each line a leading
   250	 * blockquote, line-comment, comment-continuation or bullet marker is dropped,
   251	 * JSX's `{" "}` becomes a space, and then every run of whitespace, newlines
   252	 * included, becomes one space. Returns, for each character of the result, the
   253	 * 0-based source line it came from.
   254	 *
   255	 * ⚠ **`REVIEW-058` round three (R3-5, `CLAIMS.md` E-330)**: whitespace alone
   256	 * was not enough. A copy wrapped inside a blockquote kept `> ` between its words,
   257	 * and a JSX copy wrapped after `{" "}` kept the braces, and both passed with
   258	 * the real page edited. Other markup between words, a tag or an entity or
   259	 * emphasis, still hides a copy, and the gate's printed limits say so.
   260	 */
   261	function flatten(text: string): { flat: string; lineAt: number[] } {
   262	  let flat = "";
   263	  const lineAt: number[] = [];
   264	  let inSpace = false;
   265	  text.split("\n").forEach((raw, line) => {
   266	    const body =
   267	      raw
   268	        .replace(/^\s*(?:(?:>\s*)+|\/\/+\s*|\*+\s+|-\s+)/, "")
   269	        .replace(/\{\s*(["'`])\s*\1\s*\}/g, " ") + "\n";
   270	    for (const ch of body) {
   271	      if (/\s/.test(ch)) {
   272	        if (!inSpace) {
   273	          flat += " ";
   274	          lineAt.push(line);
   275	          inSpace = true;
   276	        }
   277	        continue;
   278	      }
   279	      inSpace = false;
   280	      flat += ch;
   281	      for (let k = 0; k < ch.length; k++) lineAt.push(line);
   282	    }
   283	  });
   284	  return { flat, lineAt };
   285	}
   286	
   287	/**
   288	 * The REAL detector. Every control below calls THIS — a control that
   289	 * re-implements the check proves only that the re-implementation works
   290	 * (`CLAIMS.md` E-182).
   291	 */
   292	export function scan(extra?: { name: string; text: string }): Hit[] {
   293	  const bad: Hit[] = [];
   294	  const items: Array<[string, string]> = liveFiles().map((f) => [f, readFileSync(f, "utf8")]);
   295	  if (extra) items.push([extra.name, extra.text]);
   296	  for (const [file, text] of items) {
   297	    const lines = text.split("\n");
   298	    // ⚠⚠ **A COPY WRAPPED ACROSS TWO LINES PASSED — `REVIEW-058` R2-11,
   299	    // `CLAIMS.md` E-329.** This matched each phrase within one source line, so
   300	    // the front page's false sentence passed once a line break fell after its
   301	    // comma, and so did the wallet sentence split before "release". JSX and
   302	    // Markdown both wrap prose. The text is now flattened, every run of
   303	    // whitespace to one space, and each hit reports the line it starts on.
   304	    const { flat, lineAt } = flatten(text);
   305	    for (const r of RETRACTED) {
   306	      const needle = r.phrase.replace(/\s+/g, " ");
   307	      for (let at = flat.indexOf(needle); at >= 0; at = flat.indexOf(needle, at + 1)) {
   308	        const i = lineAt[at];
   309	        const window = lines.slice(Math.max(0, i - WINDOW), i + WINDOW + 1).join("\n");
   310	        // ⚠⚠ **A RETRACTION TOKEN IS REQUIRED, NOT MERELY A CITATION —
   311	        // `CLAIMS.md` E-238.** E-232 tightened the marker LISTS after a review
   312	        // id forgave the assertion it was added to catch; the REVIEW-037
   313	        // spot-check proved the MODE survived that fix, because a bare
   314	        // `E-224` — an ordinary cross-reference that appears for a hundred
   315	        // unrelated reasons — still satisfied `markers.some()`.
   316	        //
   317	        // ⚠ **A citation says "this was discussed". A STRIKE says "this is
   318	        // withdrawn".** Only the second may forgive a live assertion, so a hit
   319	        // is now forgiven only when the window carries BOTH a retraction token
   320	        // AND one of the phrase's own markers.
   321	        // ⚠ The phrase's own marker lists CONTAIN the retraction tokens, so a
   322	        // naive `markers.some()` let a lone `RETRACTED` satisfy BOTH halves and
   323	        // the requirement was toothless. **Caught by this gate's own new
   324	        // control, before the fix was believed.** Identity and strike must come
   325	        // from disjoint sets.
   326	        const struck = RETRACTION_TOKENS.some((m) => window.includes(m));
   327	        const cited = r.markers
   328	          .filter((m) => !RETRACTION_TOKENS.includes(m))
   329	          .some((m) => window.includes(m));
   330	        if (!(struck && cited)) {
   331	          bad.push({ file, line: i + 1, phrase: r.phrase, why: r.why });
   332	        }
   333	      }
   334	    }
   335	  }
   336	  return bad;
   337	}

   341	if (import.meta.main) {
   342	  let failures = 0;
   343	  let controls = 0;
   344	  const control = (label: string, ok: boolean) => {
   345	    controls++;
   346	    console.log(`  CONTROL ${ok ? "✓" : "✗"} ${label}`);
   347	    if (!ok) failures++;
   348	  };
   349	
   350	  console.log("check-disclosure-phrases — no live file may assert a retracted disclosure");
   351	  console.log("  (docs/reviews/ is exempt: a packet is the record of what a leg was shown)\n");
   352	
   353	  // ⚠ A gate over an EMPTY set passes trivially and says nothing. Refuse first.
   354	  if (RETRACTED.length === 0) {
   355	    console.log("FAIL: the retracted-phrase list is empty — this gate would assert nothing");
   356	    process.exit(1);
   357	  }

   361	  if (hits.length) {

   364	      console.log(`             ${h.why}`);
   365	    }

   367	  } else {

   372	  const p = RETRACTED[0];

   383	  control(

   386	  );
   387	  control(
   388	    "a retraction TOKEN alone, without the phrase's own marker, does NOT forgive",
   389	    scan({ name: "<injected>", text: `⚠ RETRACTED elsewhere\n${p.phrase}\n` }).some((h) => h.file === "<injected>"),
   390	  );
   391	  control(
   392	    "a marker OUTSIDE the window does NOT forgive the hit",
   393	    scan({
   394	      name: "<injected>",
   395	      text: `${p.markers[0]}\n${"filler\n".repeat(WINDOW + 2)}${p.phrase}\n`,
   396	    }).some((h) => h.file === "<injected>"),
   397	  );
   398	  control(
   399	    "clean prose is NOT caught",
   400	    scan({ name: "<injected>", text: "nothing retracted here at all\n" }).length === hits.length,
   401	  );
   402	  // ⚠ REVIEW-058 R2-11 and R2-12 (E-329): wrapped copies, and a true sentence
   403	  // that shares words with a retracted one.
   404	  const wrapped = p.phrase.replace(/ /, "\n");
   405	  control(
   406	    "a copy WRAPPED across two lines IS caught",
   407	    wrapped !== p.phrase &&
   408	      scan({ name: "<injected>", text: `prose\n${wrapped}\nmore prose` }).some((h) => h.file === "<injected>"),
   409	  );
   410	  control(
   411	    "a copy wrapped and INDENTED, as JSX wraps it, IS caught",
   412	    scan({
   413	      name: "<injected>",
   414	      text: "          The three reasons above cannot be\n          closed by any release.\n",
   415	    }).some((h) => h.file === "<injected>"),
   416	  );
   417	  control(
   418	    "a TRUE sentence that shares the retracted words is NOT caught",
   419	    !scan({
   420	      name: "<injected>",
   421	      text: "The protocol-mandated issuer mirror cannot be closed by any wallet update or any release.\n",
   422	    }).some((h) => h.file === "<injected>"),
   423	  );
   424	  // ⚠ R3-4 (E-330): the control above lacked each pattern's full predicate, so
   425	  // it could not protect a pattern that had lost its subject. Each of these keeps
   426	  // a wallet phrase's whole predicate and changes only the subject.
   427	  control(
   428	    "each wallet phrase's predicate, on ANOTHER subject, is NOT caught",

INDEX BUILDER
     1	/**
     2	 * build-claims-index.ts — a navigable index of `CLAIMS.md`, DERIVED.
     3	 *
     4	 * `CLAIMS.md` is 416 KB across 305 rows with a mean row of ~1,400 characters.
     5	 * It is a register, not a document: you cannot read it, you grep it. **The
     6	 * index is the thing that makes it navigable, and the only safe index is a
     7	 * generated one.**
     8	 *
     9	 * ⚠ **DERIVED, NEVER RESTATED — `CLAIMS.md` E-199, E-203, E-236.** This project
    10	 * has sixteen recorded instances of a hand-maintained number or summary going
    11	 * stale, including one that was already false in the commit that corrected it.
    12	 * A hand-written index of 305 rows would be the seventeenth before the week was
    13	 * out. So it is generated, and `--check` fails when it drifts.
    14	 *
    15	 *   bun run tools/build-claims-index.ts            # write docs/CLAIMS-INDEX.md
    16	 *   bun run tools/build-claims-index.ts --check     # fail if stale (the gate)
    17	 *
    18	 * ⚠ **What this does NOT do.** It does not judge a row, check an evidence cell,
    19	 * or verify a grade. It is a table of contents. The register's discipline lives
    20	 * in the rows and in `check-tables`, not here.
    21	 */
    22	import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
    23	import { join } from "node:path";
    24	
    25	const REPO = new URL("..", import.meta.url).pathname;
    26	const SRC = join(REPO, "CLAIMS.md");
    27	const OUT = join(REPO, "docs/CLAIMS-INDEX.md");
    28	
    29	/**
    30	 * A row id: E-1, F-24, B-15, P-12, U-54, **R-6** and **E-3a**.
    31	 *
    32	 * ⚠⚠ **THE FIRST VERSION MISSED TWO FORMS AND THE COUNT IS WHAT EXPOSED IT.**
    33	 * It read `[EFBPU]-\d+`, which (a) omitted `R-` entirely, silently dropping the
    34	 * **whole Retracted section**, and (b) truncated the SUFFIXED id `E-3a` to
    35	 * `E-3`, which then looked like a duplicate of the real `E-3` one line above.
    36	 * **A phantom defect in the register, manufactured by the indexer's own regex.**
    37	 *
    38	 * ⚠ **It was caught because the tool PRINTS its counts and they disagreed with
    39	 * the source** — 304 against 305, four sections against five. `CLAIMS.md` E-141:
    40	 * *a gate that reports a number is claiming what the number counts.* **The
    41	 * number is the falsifier; a silent index would have shipped both bugs.**
    42	 */
    43	/**
    44	 * ⚠⚠ **THE SPACE AFTER THE LEADING PIPE IS OPTIONAL IN GFM, AND REQUIRING IT
    45	 * SILENTLY DROPPED ROWS.** `|E-9999| … |` is a real table row — a parser
    46	 * confirms it — and this regex used to demand `"| "`, so such a row appeared in
    47	 * NO index, NO topic view, and no gate objected (REVIEW-040 H2).
    48	 * ⚠ **Completeness quantified over PARSED rows says nothing about a row that is
    49	 * never parsed.**
    50	 */
    51	const ROW = /^ {0,3}\|\s*(?:\*\*)?([A-Z]+-\d+[a-z]?)(?:\*\*)?\s*\|/;
    52	
    53	interface Entry {
    54	  id: string;
    55	  line: number;
    56	  section: string;
    57	  summary: string;
    58	  grade: string;
    59	}
    60	
    61	/**
    62	 * Reduce a claim cell to one scannable line.
    63	 *
    64	 * ⚠ **Markup is stripped, not rendered.** The rows carry heavy `⚠`/`⚠⚠` and
    65	 * bold emphasis that is load-bearing *in the row* and pure noise *in an index*.
    66	 * Truncation is at a word boundary so a summary never ends mid-token.
    67	 */
    68	/**
    69	 * Split a table row into cells on STRUCTURAL pipes.
    70	 *
    71	 * ⚠⚠ **A PIPE IS STRUCTURAL EVEN INSIDE A CODE SPAN — the GFM spec says so
    72	 * explicitly, and two parsers agree.** An earlier version of this function
    73	 * skipped over backtick spans, which made the generators disagree with the
    74	 * renderer in the opposite direction from the bug they were fixing
    75	 * (`REVIEW-041`). **Only `\\|` is content.**
    76	 *
    77	 * ⚠ **The register was the thing that was wrong**, not the splitter: five rows
    78	 * carried unescaped pipes inside code spans and rendered with the wrong Grade.
    79	 * They are escaped now, and `check-table-integrity` counts the same way this
    80	 * does, so a regression fails the gate.
    81	 */
    82	export function splitCells(line: string): string[] {
    83	  const out: string[] = [];
    84	  let cur = "";
    85	  let i = 0;
    86	  while (i < line.length) {
    87	    // ⚠ **A `|` PRECEDED BY A BACKSLASH IS CONTENT — one character of lookback,
    88	    // no escaped-backslash counting.** This used to treat `\\` as escaping the
    89	    // backslash, making the pipe in `\\|` structural; `cmark-gfm` and Pandoc
    90	    // both treat it as escaped (`REVIEW-042`). Validated cell-for-cell against
    91	    // `cmark-gfm 0.29.0.gfm.13` over twelve row shapes.
    92	    if (line[i] === "\\" && line[i + 1] === "|") { cur += "\\|"; i += 2; continue; }
    93	    if (line[i] === "|") { out.push(cur); cur = ""; i++; continue; }
    94	    cur += line[i];
    95	    i++;
    96	  }
    97	  out.push(cur);
    98	  return out;
    99	}
   100	
   101	
   102	
   103	/**
   104	 * The CONTENT cells of a row: `splitCells` minus the empties that flank a row
   105	 * written with outer pipes.
   106	 *
   107	 * ⚠⚠ **A trailing pipe is OPTIONAL in GFM, and assuming one shifted the grade by
   108	 * a cell.** `| E-1 | claim | ev | A \|` ends in an ESCAPED pipe — content, not a
   109	 * delimiter — so there is no trailing empty, and `cells[length - 2]` read the
   110	 * EVIDENCE as the grade. `check-table-integrity` correctly passes such a row:
   111	 * it is valid GFM with four cells (REVIEW-041 leg A, defect 2.2).
   112	 */
   113	export function contentCells(line: string): string[] {
   114	  const parts = splitCells(line);
   115	  if (parts.length && parts[0].trim() === "") parts.shift();
   116	  if (parts.length && parts[parts.length - 1].trim() === "") parts.pop();
   117	  return parts;
   118	}
   119	
   120	export function summarise(cell: string, max = 120): string {
   121	  const flat = cell
   122	    .replace(/⚠+/g, "")
   123	    .replace(/\*\*/g, "")
   124	    .replace(/`/g, "")
   125	    // ⚠ STRIKES ARE KEPT, NOT DELETED (R-9, 2026-10-22). Deleting `~~` turned a
   126	    // struck quotation into an unstruck one: F-9's headline read *"cannot be
   127	    // resolved from public remotes does not resolve"*, and R-9's retracted phrase
   128	    // reached three topic files as an assertion, which `check-disclosure-phrases`
   129	    // caught. A strike in the register is a strike in its excerpt.
   130	    .replace(/\[([^\]]+)\]\([^)]*\)/g, "$1")
   131	    // ⚠⚠ **A PIPE IN A HEADLINE BECOMES A CELL BOUNDARY IN THE GENERATED ROW.**
   132	    // Backticks are stripped above, so `` `a|b|c` `` — an ordinary grep
   133	    // alternation in this register — used to emit `a|b|c` and break the very
   134	    // table this index is made of (REVIEW-040 M6). Escape, do not delete: the
   135	    // pipe is content and the reader should see it.
   136	    // ⚠⚠ **NORMALISE, THEN ESCAPE ONCE.** Escaping every `|` turned a source
   137	    // `\|` — already an escape — into `\\|`, which renders as a literal
   138	    // backslash followed by a STRUCTURAL pipe, adding a cell to the generated
   139	    // row (REVIEW-041 leg A, question 5). Unescape first so the count is one.
   140	    .replace(/\\\|/g, "|")
   141	    .replace(/\|/g, "\\|")
   142	    .replace(/\s+/g, " ")
   143	    .trim();
   144	  if (flat.length <= max) return flat;
   145	  const cut = flat.slice(0, max);
   146	  const sp = cut.lastIndexOf(" ");
   147	  const kept = (sp > max * 0.6 ? cut.slice(0, sp) : cut).trimEnd();
   148	  // A cut inside a strike would leave it open and strike the rest of the row.
   149	  const open = (kept.match(/~~/g) ?? []).length % 2 === 1;
   150	  return kept + "…" + (open ? "~~" : "");
   151	}
   152	
   153	export function parse(text: string): Entry[] {
   154	  const out: Entry[] = [];
   155	  let section = "(none)";
   156	  const lines = text.split("\n");
   157	  for (let i = 0; i < lines.length; i++) {
   158	    const l = lines[i];
   159	    const h = l.match(/^## (.+)$/);
   160	    if (h) { section = h[1].replace(/[*`]/g, "").trim(); continue; }
   161	    const m = l.match(ROW);
   162	    if (!m) continue;
   163	    // Cells: leading "" | id | claim | evidence | grade | trailing ""
   164	    const cells = contentCells(l).map((c) => c.trim());
   165	    const claim = cells[1] ?? "";
   166	    const grade = (cells.length >= 3 ? cells[cells.length - 1] : "") ?? "";
   167	    out.push({
   168	      id: m[1],
   169	      line: i + 1,
   170	      section,
   171	      summary: summarise(claim),
   172	      grade: summarise(grade, 22) || "—",
   173	    });
   174	  }
   175	  return out;
   176	}
   177	
   178	export function render(entries: Entry[]): string {
   179	  const bySection = new Map<string, Entry[]>();
   180	  for (const e of entries) {
   181	    if (!bySection.has(e.section)) bySection.set(e.section, []);
   182	    bySection.get(e.section)!.push(e);
   183	  }
   184	  const L: string[] = [
   185	    "# CLAIMS index",
   186	    "",
   187	    "⚠⚠ **GENERATED. DO NOT HAND-EDIT.** Rebuild with `bun run tools/build-claims-index.ts`;",
   188	    "`make check-claims-index` fails if this file drifts from `CLAIMS.md`.",
   189	    "",
   190	    "**Why it exists:** `CLAIMS.md` is a register of hundreds of rows averaging over a",
   191	    "thousand characters each. It is not readable end to end and was never meant to be —",
   192	    "this is how you find a row. **Line numbers link into the file and are regenerated,**",
   193	    "so they do not rot the way a hand-written index would (`CLAIMS.md` E-199, E-236).",
   194	    "",
   195	    "⚠ **A summary is not a claim.** Each line below is a truncated, markup-stripped",
   196	    "excerpt for finding things. **The row is the authority** — never cite the index.",
   197	    "",
   198	    `**${entries.length} rows** across **${bySection.size} sections**, counted where they are parsed.`,
   199	    "",
   200	  ];
   201	  for (const [section, rows] of bySection) {
   202	    L.push(`## ${section} — ${rows.length} rows`, "");
   203	    L.push("| id | summary | grade |", "|---|---|---|");
   204	    for (const e of rows) {
   205	      L.push(`| [${e.id}](../CLAIMS.md#L${e.line}) | ${e.summary} | ${e.grade} |`);
   206	    }
   207	    L.push("");
   208	  }
   209	  return L.join("\n");
   210	}

513:| R-6 | B-11 / ADR-0002 blocker 3 / investigation §12: that encrypted loan accounting is **structurally** blocked, because XLS-96's additive homomorphism "cannot support amortisation, which multiplies a balance by a rate" | Withdrawn 2026-08-17. The residual true statement is B-11 as rewritten | **The mathematics was wrong.** Scalar multiplication by a *public* scalar is native to an additively homomorphic scheme: for `(C₁,C₂) = (rG, mG+rP)`, scaling both components by public `k` yields `(krG, kmG+krP)`, which decrypts to `k·m`. R9 CONTEXT
    80	
    81	A bank converts a float into confidential form, then draws down to suppliers
    82	**A**, **B** and **C**. Later they repay, and the facility retires in tranches.
    83	
    84	**An outside observer learns:**
    85	
    86	- the size of the float, exactly
    87	- that A, B and C each deal with the bank, and on which days
    88	- how often each of them transacts
    89	- the size of every retirement tranche
    90	- the total outstanding at any moment
    91	
    92	**They do not learn:**
    93	
    94	- A's credit limit
    95	- what B drew down last Tuesday
    96	- what C still owes
    97	
    98	⚠ **And crucially, A cannot see B's terms.** In receivables finance the
    99	commercially sensitive facts are per-counterparty pricing and exposure, and
   100	those are genuinely hidden. **That is the real product.**
   101	
   102	---
   103	
   104	## The three limits, stated plainly
   105	
   106	**1. The public perimeter constrains the hidden interior — by arithmetic, not by
   107	decryption.**
   108	
   109	If a holder converts in 500, receives nothing, and converts back 400, ~~then 100
   110	left by transfer~~ the other 100 is either still held or has left by confidential
   111	transfer (corrected 2026-10-21, `CLAIMS.md` R-7). Anyone can do that subtraction. No key required. The public
   112	edges and totals **bound** the hidden values, and in a small enough system they
   113	pin them exactly.
   114	
   115	**2. The exit is granular, not aggregate.**
   116	
   117	⚠ **This project got this wrong in its own walkthrough and had to correct it.**
   118	Retiring in tranches publishes **every tranche size**, because the amount is a
   119	plaintext field on each individual `ConvertBack` — not a single netted figure at
   120	the end. Two tranches on our own Devnet ledger read **95** and **191**, legible
   121	to anyone (`CLAIMS.md` **F-24**).
   122	
   123	**3. The issuer reads everything, always.**
   124	
   125	The decryption mirror is mandatory and no configuration removes it. ⚠ **So this
   126	is confidentiality from the public, never from the counterparty with the most
   127	reason to look** (**P-9**).
   128	
   129	---
   130	
   131	## The sentence to use
   132	
   133	> **It hides how much each supplier draws and owes, not who borrows, when, or the
   134	> size of the float.**
   135	
   136	⚠ This said ~~*"It hides the shape of the book, not the size of the book"*~~ until
   137	2026-10-22. A reader new to the project took *shape* to mean who borrows and when,
   138	which is public, so it overstated the privacy (`CLAIMS.md` R-9).
   139	
   140	That is real, and it is a good deal less than "confidential positions" sounds
   141	like — which is why [`README.md`](../../README.md) states what is **public** as
   142	plainly as what is hidden.
   143	
   144	⚠ **If you need the amounts entering and leaving to be private too, this
   145	protocol does not do that**, and no configuration of it will.

INDEX FUNCTIONS
   105	 * written with outer pipes.
   106	 *
   107	 * ⚠⚠ **A trailing pipe is OPTIONAL in GFM, and assuming one shifted the grade by
   108	 * a cell.** `| E-1 | claim | ev | A \|` ends in an ESCAPED pipe — content, not a
   109	 * delimiter — so there is no trailing empty, and `cells[length - 2]` read the
   110	 * EVIDENCE as the grade. `check-table-integrity` correctly passes such a row:
   111	 * it is valid GFM with four cells (REVIEW-041 leg A, defect 2.2).
   112	 */
   113	export function contentCells(line: string): string[] {
   114	  const parts = splitCells(line);
   115	  if (parts.length && parts[0].trim() === "") parts.shift();
   116	  if (parts.length && parts[parts.length - 1].trim() === "") parts.pop();
   117	  return parts;
   118	}
   119	
   120	export function summarise(cell: string, max = 120): string {
   121	  const flat = cell
   122	    .replace(/⚠+/g, "")
   123	    .replace(/\*\*/g, "")
   124	    .replace(/`/g, "")
   125	    // ⚠ STRIKES ARE KEPT, NOT DELETED (R-9, 2026-10-22). Deleting `~~` turned a
   126	    // struck quotation into an unstruck one: F-9's headline read *"cannot be
   127	    // resolved from public remotes does not resolve"*, and R-9's retracted phrase
   128	    // reached three topic files as an assertion, which `check-disclosure-phrases`
   129	    // caught. A strike in the register is a strike in its excerpt.
   130	    .replace(/\[([^\]]+)\]\([^)]*\)/g, "$1")
   131	    // ⚠⚠ **A PIPE IN A HEADLINE BECOMES A CELL BOUNDARY IN THE GENERATED ROW.**
   132	    // Backticks are stripped above, so `` `a|b|c` `` — an ordinary grep
   133	    // alternation in this register — used to emit `a|b|c` and break the very
   134	    // table this index is made of (REVIEW-040 M6). Escape, do not delete: the
   135	    // pipe is content and the reader should see it.
   136	    // ⚠⚠ **NORMALISE, THEN ESCAPE ONCE.** Escaping every `|` turned a source
   137	    // `\|` — already an escape — into `\\|`, which renders as a literal
   138	    // backslash followed by a STRUCTURAL pipe, adding a cell to the generated
   139	    // row (REVIEW-041 leg A, question 5). Unescape first so the count is one.
   140	    .replace(/\\\|/g, "|")
   141	    .replace(/\|/g, "\\|")
   142	    .replace(/\s+/g, " ")
   143	    .trim();
   144	  if (flat.length <= max) return flat;
   145	  const cut = flat.slice(0, max);
   146	  const sp = cut.lastIndexOf(" ");
   147	  const kept = (sp > max * 0.6 ? cut.slice(0, sp) : cut).trimEnd();
   148	  // A cut inside a strike would leave it open and strike the rest of the row.
   149	  const open = (kept.match(/~~/g) ?? []).length % 2 === 1;
   150	  return kept + "…" + (open ? "~~" : "");
   151	}
   152	
   153	export function parse(text: string): Entry[] {
   154	  const out: Entry[] = [];
   155	  let section = "(none)";
   156	  const lines = text.split("\n");
   157	  for (let i = 0; i < lines.length; i++) {
   158	    const l = lines[i];
   159	    const h = l.match(/^## (.+)$/);
   160	    if (h) { section = h[1].replace(/[*`]/g, "").trim(); continue; }
   161	    const m = l.match(ROW);
   162	    if (!m) continue;
   163	    // Cells: leading "" | id | claim | evidence | grade | trailing ""
   164	    const cells = contentCells(l).map((c) => c.trim());
   165	    const claim = cells[1] ?? "";

Separately, **F-12 is the only item here that is cheap, uncontested and fileable today**: a one-flag build fix with a reproduction on two emsdk versions, no dependency on any other open question. If exactly one thing goes upstream from this session, it is F-12.
   500

   506	
   507	| # | Was claimed | Corrected to | Why |
   508	|---|---|---|---|
   509	| R-1 | TASK ZERO §9 rev 1: the restructured facility "shows nothing about which supplier drew how much" | Amounts are hidden; counterparty graph, event timing and drawdown frequency are public | Found independently by all three review passes. Sender and receiver are public on every transfer |
   510	| R-2 | ADR-0001 rev 1: local proving is "the only option under which the confidentiality claim is true" | Local proving preserves spending authority; issuer visibility is unchanged | Conflated custody with confidentiality — the exact distinction the ADR exists to draw |
   511	| R-3 | F-3: "docs say confidentiality can be toggled on and off" | Withdrawn 2026-08-16 | Corrected upstream. The canonical xrpl.org page states enabling is one-way |
   512	| R-4 | F-4: "docs say clawback resets the version counter" | Withdrawn 2026-08-16 | Not a doc error. TOB-RIPCTX-11, a Medium implementation bug found by Trail of Bits in April 2026 and since Resolved. The prerelease docs described pre-fix behaviour |
   513	| R-6 | B-11 / ADR-0002 blocker 3 / investigation §12: that encrypted loan accounting is **structurally** blocked, because XLS-96's additive homomorphism "cannot support amortisation, which multiplies a balance by a rate" | Withdrawn 2026-08-17. The residual true statement is B-11 as rewritten | **The mathematics was wrong.** Scalar multiplication by a *public* scalar is native to an additively homomorphic scheme: for `(C₁,C₂) = (rG, mG+rP)`, scaling both components by public `k` yields `(krG, kmG+krP)`, which decrypts to `k·m`. An interest rate is a public loan parameter. What is genuinely non-linear is rounding and fixed-point truncation — and the remedy for that is a per-payment ZK proof, which is the pattern XLS-96 already uses. **Found independently by both REVIEW-003 legs**, and verified algebraically before acceptance. It was graded C and its inference was stated, which is what made it checkable — but a stated inference that is wrong is still wrong |
   514	| R-5 | TASK ZERO §9: the vault converts the whole facility float in one transaction | ~~Retracted 2026-08-16 per ADDENDUM §1~~ — **un-retracted 2026-08-16 (same day), see F-7** | The retraction was correct about the mechanism and wrong about the consequence. A 10,000,000-unit balance is **not** undecryptable: decryption takes a caller-supplied window, and the vault — which tracks its own float off-ledger anyway — decrypts it in ~5 ms with a narrow window. §9's single-conversion design **stands**. What must be added is not a float ceiling but a **balance-tracking requirement** and a resynchronisation cost budget |
   515	| R-7 | `docs/explainer/WHAT-CONFIDENTIAL-MEANS-2026-09-02.md`, limit 1, and the README before 2026-10-19: a holder who converts in 500, receives nothing and converts back 400 shows that *"100 left by transfer"* | The other 100 is either still held or has left by confidential transfer. The arithmetic bounds the balance and does not say which. Corrected in the explainer on 2026-10-21 | The README's rewrite for publication (`c561541`, 2026-10-19) carried the corrected sentence with no row, and the explainer the README links for the long form kept the old one, public from that day. Found on 2026-10-21 while drafting the hosted site's explainer from both. The error overstated what an observer learns, not what is hidden |
   516	| R-8 | `web/api/capability.ts`'s wallet row and the wallet page: *"A confidential transaction needs the ElGamal secret and the account key"*, and *"needs two secrets"* | A Send, a ConvertBack and the first Convert, which registers the key, need both; a MergeInbox or a later Convert needs only the account key (TASK ZERO §3), and the facility signs its MergeInbox with the seed alone. The wallet conclusion stands, because without the first Convert there is no position. Corrected 2026-10-22 | Found by `REVIEW-061` leg A in a diagram caption that repeated the sentence. Both copies had been on the public site since publication; earlier reads of the wallet page checked its conclusion, which holds, and not this premise |
   517	| R-9 | The hosted explainer `/how-it-works`, `README.md` and `WHAT-CONFIDENTIAL-MEANS`, the last as *"the sentence to use"*: ~~*"it hides the shape of the book, not its size"*~~ | *"It hides how much each supplier draws and owes, not who borrows, when, or the size of the float."* Replaced 2026-10-22, and `check-disclosure-phrases` now refuses the old wording unless it is struck beside this id | True as the register meant it, the per-supplier amounts against the public totals. `REVIEW-062`'s leg B, reading the draft blog post as a stranger, took *shape* to mean who borrows, when and how often, which is public, so the sentence overstated the privacy in the direction P-4 and P-11 forbid. It was in the README and `WHAT-CONFIDENTIAL-MEANS` from 2026-09-02 (`00b5478`) and on the hosted explainer from E-350, and every earlier read passed it, because each read it as its row |

FACILITY WALKTHROUGH
     1	# A confidential receivables facility on the XRPL — how it actually works
     2	
     3	**Date:** 2026-08-20, **revised twice on 2026-08-25 and once on 2026-08-28**
     4	(§5's zero-balance nuance for `CLAIMS.md` **E-211**, §6's build table for the
     5	web tier, and the amendment reading re-dated) — §3 step 4 and §4's table
     6	for `CLAIMS.md` **F-26** (a second false disclosure sentence in this document),
     7	§3 step 9 and §4's table for **F-24**, and §6's build table after architecture
     8	§6 step 7 was **built and executed**. **Devnet only.** Written as the reference
     9	an app, an explainer or a post would be built *from* — not as any of those.
    10	
    11	⚠ **The facility now runs, and the row in §6 carries a qualification that must
    12	travel with it**: the run was **not** under `CLAIMS.md` B-15's step-7
    13	conditions, because the ledger source was remote under an amended ruling
    14	(E-151). It is evidence that the transactions are well-formed and that rippled
    15	accepts them. It is **not** evidence about the loopback obligation.
    16	
    17	> ## ⚠ Read this box before reusing anything below
    18	>
    19	> **This has not been through the project's publishing protocol.** That protocol
    20	> is deliberately not part of a coding session, and nothing here is cleared for
    21	> external use. Every capability sentence below is written against
    22	> `CLAIMS.md`'s standing prohibitions, and the register is the authority if the
    23	> two ever disagree.
    24	>
    25	> **The one sentence that must survive any rewrite:** this design hides
    26	> **amounts**. It does not hide **who** transacts, **with whom**, **when**, or
    27	> **how often**, and the issuer can decrypt every balance by construction. An
    28	> explainer that leaves that out is not a simplification of this document; it is
    29	> a different and false claim.
    30	
    31	---
    32	
    33	## 1. The commercial problem, in one paragraph
    34	
    35	A large buyer's suppliers want to be paid early; a bank will advance against the
    36	buyer's payables. That is receivables financing, and the numbers in it are
    37	commercially sensitive in a specific way: **a supplier's drawdown level tells you
    38	their cash position.** Put that on a public ledger in plaintext and you have
    39	published every supplier's working-capital stress to their competitors and to
    40	the buyer's other counterparties. Put it on a private ledger and you have given
    41	up most of what a shared ledger was for.
    42	
    43	**XLS-0096 Confidential MPTs are an attempt at the middle**: amounts encrypted
    44	on a public chain, with a decryption path reserved for the parties who are
    45	accountable for the book.
    46	
    47	## 2. The shape
    48	
    49	Three roles, **one issuance**, and every participant holds a confidential
    50	balance in it.
    51	
    52	```
    53	      ┌────────────────────────┐
    54	      │  Funding bank          │  issuer of the MPT
    55	      │  · IssuerEncryptionKey │  ── can decrypt EVERY balance, always
    56	      │  · AuditorEncryptionKey│  ── optional second party, same power
    57	      └───────────┬────────────┘
    58	                  │ funds publicly, once
    59	                  ▼
    60	      ┌────────────────────────┐
    61	      │  Dedicated Account     │  an ORDINARY XRPL account
    62	      │  holds the float,      │  (not an XLS-65 Vault — see §7)
    63	      │  confidentially        │
    64	      └───────────┬────────────┘
    65	                  │  ConfidentialMPTSend — amounts hidden
    66	        ┌─────────┼─────────┬─────────┐
    67	        ▼         ▼         ▼         ▼
    68	     supplier  supplier  supplier   ...        each with its own
    69	        A         B         C                  HolderEncryptionKey
    70	```
    71	
    72	⚠ **"Dedicated Account", never "vault".** An XLS-65 `Vault` is a different
    73	ledger object, it *cannot* convert to a confidential balance, and the word has
    74	already nearly derailed one reading of the design.
    75	
    76	## 3. The walkthrough
    77	
    78	A worked example: a bank runs a **£50m** facility for **30 suppliers** of one
    79	large buyer.
    80	
    81	### Setup — public, and deliberately so
    82	
    83	**Step 1 — the bank creates the issuance.** A Multi-Purpose Token flagged to
    84	hold confidential balances. It sets:
    85	
    86	- **`IssuerEncryptionKey`** — mandatory. The bank can decrypt every holder's
    87	  balance. **No configuration removes this**, and any design that assumes
    88	  otherwise is wrong about the protocol.
    89	- **`AuditorEncryptionKey`** — optional. A trustee or supervisor with the same
    90	  visibility.
    91	- **`sfDomainID`** — gates the issuance to a permissioned domain, so only
    92	  credentialled accounts can hold it.
    93	
    94	⚠ **`TransferFee` must be zero on a confidential issuance.** Fees and interest
    95	settle off-ledger or as separate confidential transfers. That is a protocol
    96	constraint, not a design choice, and it shapes everything downstream.
    97	
    98	**Step 2 — the bank creates a Dedicated Account.** An ordinary XRPL account.
    99	It cannot be the issuer account: **an issuer cannot convert its own issuance
   100	into a confidential balance.** The ledger refuses it outright — this is the
   101	reason the design needs a separate account to hold the float, not a stylistic
   102	preference.
   103	
   104	**Step 3 — the bank funds it publicly** with the whole £50m float, as plaintext
   105	MPT.
   106	
   107	### The one plaintext moment
   108	
   109	**Step 4 — one `ConfidentialMPTConvert`.** This does two things at once: it
   110	registers the Dedicated Account's `HolderEncryptionKey`, and it moves the entire
   111	float into confidentiality.
   112	
   113	**The amount is public at this step, and that is the intent.** Facility size is
   114	what the market and the funders are entitled to see.
   115	
   116	⚠ **~~After this, no plaintext amount appears again until the facility is
   117	retired or resized.~~ That sentence was FALSE and is struck (2026-08-25,
   118	`CLAIMS.md` F-26).** Step 5 publishes two plaintext amounts **per supplier** —
   119	the bank's `Payment` of the enrolment token, and the supplier's own
   120	`ConfidentialMPTConvert`, whose `MPTAmount` is a plaintext field exactly as step
   121	4's and step 9's are. On a thirty-supplier facility that is sixty plaintext
   122	amounts between the float conversion and the first drawdown.
   123	
   124	**What is true, and it is what the design actually buys:** no **drawdown** and
   125	no **repayment** publishes an amount, and those are the numbers that carry the
   126	commercial signal. The plaintext amounts are the enrolment tokens, which are
   127	deliberately nominal and identical, and the facility-level ones — its size, and
   128	each tranche of its retirement.
   129	
   130	⚠ This is the **second** false disclosure sentence found in this document
   131	(F-24 was the first), and like F-24 it survived the document's own
   132	`claims-check`. Both were about *which* amounts are plaintext. A sentence of the
   133	form *"no plaintext amount appears after X"* should be assumed wrong until every
   134	transaction type between X and the end has been listed.
   135	
   136	### Enrolling a supplier
   137	
   138	**Step 5.** The bank pays the supplier a token amount of the MPT publicly, and
   139	the supplier runs its own `ConfidentialMPTConvert` — which is what registers
   140	their `HolderEncryptionKey`.
   141	
   142	⚠ **Registration happens exactly once and cannot be repeated.** The protocol
   143	requires the key when initialising and forbids it afterwards. A supplier with no
   144	registered key **cannot receive a confidential amount at all** — there is no key
   145	to encrypt to, so the transaction cannot be built, let alone rejected.
   146	
   147	### Running the facility
   148	
   149	**Step 6 — drawdown.** Dedicated Account → supplier, one `ConfidentialMPTSend`.
   150	The amount is hidden. Received value lands in the supplier's **inbox**; a
   151	`ConfidentialMPTMergeInbox` moves it into their spendable balance.
   152	
   153	**Step 7 — repayment.** Supplier → Dedicated Account, the same transaction type,
   154	amount hidden.
   155	
   156	**Step 8 — several funders?** They are confidential holders in the same
   157	issuance. The bank sends each their position confidentially, and yield as
   158	further confidential transfers. **No shares and no share price** — positions are
   159	denominated directly, which is a large part of why a `Vault` buys nothing here
   160	(§7).
   161	
   162	### Wind-down
   163	
   164	**Step 9 — `ConfidentialMPTConvertBack`** when the facility retires or resizes.
   165	
   166	⚠ **Public: each ConvertBack's OWN amount, in the clear — not merely the
   167	aggregate change.** ~~Public: the aggregate change.~~ **Corrected 2026-08-25
   168	(`CLAIMS.md` F-24), and the earlier sentence would have misled a reader in a way
   169	that matters:** `MPTAmount` is a plaintext field on every individual
   170	`ConfidentialMPTConvertBack` (XLS-0096 §10.3), so retiring a facility in tranches
   171	publishes **every tranche size**, not just the net movement in
   172	`sfConfidentialOutstandingAmount`. Two ConvertBacks executed on 2026-08-24 read
   173	95 and 191 straight off their validated transactions.
   174	
   175	This is symmetric with step 4: **`Convert` and `ConvertBack` are the two
   176	transaction types in this design that publish an amount, and both publish it per
   177	transaction.** It is the specification's own intent — §10.7's worked example
   178	turns on it — and not a defect.
   179	
   180	---
   181	
   182	## 4. Who sees what
   183	
   184	| | Facility size | Who is enrolled | Who drew, when, how often | **Amounts** |
   185	|---|---|---|---|---|
   186	| Anyone with a block explorer | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ for drawdowns and repayments — **but every `Convert` amount, every `ConvertBack` amount and every plaintext `Payment` is public** (F-24, F-26). That is the facility's size, each retirement tranche, **and both plaintext amounts of every enrolment** |
   187	| A supplier | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | only their own |
   188	| **The bank (issuer)** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | **✅ everyone's** |
   189	| **An auditor, if configured** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | **✅ everyone's** |
   190	
   191	**Three tiers of disclosure, and none of them requires publishing a position:**
   192	
   193	1. **Public** — `sfConfidentialOutstandingAmount` on the issuance keeps the
   194	   aggregate visible, alongside the transaction graph.
   195	2. **The arranger** — the mandatory issuer mirror.
   196	3. **A supervisor or trustee** — the optional auditor key.
   197	
   198	⚠ **This is a statement about who can decrypt what. It is not a compliance
   199	claim.** Nothing here asserts that the structure satisfies any named
   200	jurisdiction's requirements.
   201	
   202	## 5. ⚠ What this does NOT hide
   203	
   204	The most important section in this document, and the one most likely to be cut
   205	from a shorter version.
   206	
   207	**It hides the amount of a confidential *transfer*, and balances. It hides nothing else** — and ⚠ **converting in or out publishes the amount in plaintext, every time.** Only a `Send` hides one.
   208	
   209	- **The counterparty set is public.** Every supplier on the facility is
   210	  identifiable.
   211	- **Timing and frequency are public.** Every drawdown and repayment is a visible
   212	  event with a timestamp.
   213	- **Therefore drawdown *frequency* leaks.** A supplier moving from monthly to
   214	  weekly draws is **legible as distress without a single amount being known** —
   215	  which is a substantial part of the commercial signal the design set out to
   216	  protect.
   217	- **No holder is private from the issuer.** By construction, permanently.
   218	
   219	**The proposed mitigation for the frequency leak — scheduled cover traffic, so
   220	the Dedicated Account sends to every supplier on a fixed cadence whether or not
   221	value moves — is `Proposed` and has been reviewed by nobody.** It rests on
   222	zero-amount sends being indistinguishable from real ones, which this project has
   223	tested three ways and **has not established**. Surviving three attempts to break
   224	a claim is not a proof of it. Do not present cover traffic as a feature.
   225	
   226	⚠ **One thing this section did NOT say, added 2026-08-28 (`CLAIMS.md` E-211):**
   227	**a balance can be exactly zero and not publicly identifiable as zero.** F-1's
   228	canonical `EncZero` is used on first-time init, merge reset and clawback — so a
   229	freshly-enrolled supplier's balance **is** publicly known to be zero, while a
   230	supplier who has drawn and fully repaid holds a *randomised* encryption of zero
   231	that matches nothing. **The two look completely different to an observer and
   232	are the same number.** ⚠ The converse is the trap: **a ciphertext that does not
   233	match the canonical zero is NOT evidence of a non-zero balance**, and the web
   234	tier shipped a sentence saying it was.
   235	
   236	**And two protocol constraints that shape any product built on this:**
   237	
   238	- **Keys cannot be rotated or recovered.** A lost key is a permanently lost
   239	  balance; a compromised key is permanently compromised.
   240	- **Clawback, where the issuance enables it, burns the holder's *entire*
   241	  balance.** It cannot model partial recovery. It is a sanctions instrument,
   242	  not a repayment mechanism. (It is available only if the issuance carries
   243	  `lsfMPTCanClawback`; without that flag the attempt is refused — a
   244	  qualification `claims-check` caught missing here.)
   245	
   246	## 6. What is actually built, as of 2026-08-25
   247	
   248	Honest status, because an explainer that blurs *demonstrated* into *designed* is
   249	the failure this project exists to avoid.
   250

FILING RULE
    25	---
    26	
    27	## The two commands
    28	
    29	- **`/upstream-issue`** — drafts a filing from a verified finding.
    30	- **`/issue-review`** — attacks the draft before it is sent. **Rule 1 gates on it.**
    31	
    32	⚠ Both are slash commands in `.claude/commands/`, matching this project's three
    33	existing ones — **user-invoked, never model-invoked**, because filing needs
    34	authorisation every time.
    35	
    36	⚠ **Both read the target repository's issue template first**, and that outranks
    37	anything here. **Measured 2026-09-01:** `XRPLF/rippled` sets
    38	`blank_issues_enabled: false` and offers only `bug_report.md` and
    39	`feature_request.md`; `XRPL-Standards`, `xrpl-dev-portal` and `mpt-crypto` have
    40	none. ⚠⚠ **`rippled#8118` fit neither rippled template, was filed anyway, and
    41	was closed without comment.** Reading the template first would have stopped that
    42	filing before it was written — which makes it the cheapest rule here and the one
    43	that was missing.
    44	
    45	---
    46	
    47	## The five rules
    48	
    49	### 1. Adversarial review runs BEFORE filing, and it gates
    50	
    51	No filing is sent until an independent adversarial pass has run against the
    52	**draft text and the frozen primary sources**, and every finding is resolved.
    53	
    54	⚠ **A review that runs after submission cannot prevent anything.** It can only
    55	produce a correction, and a correction is a public record that the filing was
    56	not ready.
    57	
    58	**The reviewer is given the draft and the sources, not the conclusion.**
    59	
    60	### 2. A filing is at most 300 words, with one concrete ask
    61	
    62	Counted over the issue body, excluding code blocks, quoted source and the
    63	disclosure footer.
    64	
    65	⚠ **`WORD_LIMIT` in `tools/check-filing.ts` is what enforces this, and the gate
    66	prints the number it used.** This heading states the rule; that constant is the
    67	instrument. If the two ever disagree, the gate is right and this line is the
    68	defect — and neither the skills nor a draft may restate the number at all.
    69	
    70	- **One ask per issue.** If there are five asks, that is five issues or one

NEGATIVE CLAIMS GATE
#!/usr/bin/env bun
/**
 * check-negative-claims.ts — a gate for the sentence shape that has failed
 * three times, twice in a single day.
 *
 *   bun run tools/check-negative-claims.ts
 *
 * ## What this is for
 *
 * `UPSTREAM-FEEDBACK.md` is built almost entirely out of statements of the form
 * *"the source does not say X"* — nothing documents it, no field exists, it is
 * not exported, nobody has called it out. Each one is an assertion about a
 * whole corpus, and each one is falsified by a single search.
 *
 * On 2026-08-26, three graded rows failed exactly this way (E-155, E-156):
 *
 *   U-15  quoted a sentence XLS-0096 has never contained, at any revision.
 *   U-12  said a property was "not called out as a selling point anywhere I
 *         found". The spec states it TWICE, once in wording identical to the
 *         benefit claimed as an original reading.
 *   U-10  said "nothing in the documentation says so" about a dependency the
 *         canonical docs document in two places.
 *
 * ⚠ **The reason this shape survives review is that it does not look like a
 * claim.** A quotation has quotation marks to trigger suspicion. A benchmark
 * number visibly wants a methodology. "Nobody has documented this" reads as
 * modesty, and both a self-review and an external reviewer can slide past it.
 *
 * So the gate is not "review harder". It is: **a row asserting a negative must
 * carry the search that would falsify it, in the row.**
 *
 * ## What counts as a falsifier
 *
 * A recorded search a later reader can re-run or check: a `grep`/`rg` command,
 * an explicit occurrence count ("0 occurrences", "zero matches"), a named file
 * plus line, or a dated check against a named source. Prose confidence is not a
 * falsifier. Neither is a grade.
 *
 * ## Scope, and why `Observed` is exempt
 *
 * `CLAUDE.md` requires `Observed` rows to be captured at the moment of friction,
 * ungraded and unresearched — demanding a falsifier there would fight the
 * capture rule and lose. The gate therefore binds the sections where a claim has
 * passed the bar: anything Filed, Ready to file, graded, or offered as Positive.
 * `Observed` rows are reported as advisory only.
 *
 * ⚠ **This gate reports a number, and E-141 is the standing warning that a gate
 * reporting a number is making a claim about what the number counts.** Its own
 * detection is therefore pinned by SELF_TESTS below, which run before it will
 * report anything. If the detectors break, this exits non-zero without grading
 * a single row.
 */

import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

/**
 * Phrases that assert something is absent from a corpus.
 *
 * ⚠ **Each pattern is PAIRED with a probe string that only it should match.**
 * An earlier version kept the patterns in a bare list and self-tested them
 * against whole sentences; breaking one pattern did not fail the tests, because
 * a second pattern matched the same sentence. That is a false-pass mode in the
 * gate's own test — `CLAUDE.md`'s round-two lesson, reproduced here at the cost
 * of one revert. Pairing each pattern with its own probe is what makes a broken
 * detector detectable.
 */
const NEGATIVE_MARKERS: { pattern: RegExp; probe: string }[] = [
  { pattern: /\bnothing (?:in|about|says|said|forces|prevents|collects)\b/i, probe: "nothing in the docs" },
  { pattern: /\bno (?:mention|such field|corresponding|error|warning|counterpart|way|canonical|published|separate)\b/i, probe: "there is no mention" },
  { pattern: /\bnot (?:called out|advertised|documented|exported|stated|specified|published|surfaced|mentioned)\b/i, probe: "it is not advertised" },
  { pattern: /\b(?:does|do|did) not (?:exist|say|state|mention|appear|surface|document)\b/i, probe: "the field does not exist" },
  { pattern: /\bis silent\b/i, probe: "the spec is silent" },
  { pattern: /\bnowhere\b/i, probe: "it appears nowhere" },
  { pattern: /\bundocumented\b/i, probe: "an undocumented hazard" },
  { pattern: /\bnever (?:says|stated|mentions|documented)\b/i, probe: "the header never says" },
  { pattern: /\b(?:I|we) (?:could not|did not|couldn't|didn't) find\b/i, probe: "we could not find it" },
  { pattern: /\banywhere (?:I|we) (?:found|looked)\b/i, probe: "anywhere I looked" },

interface Row {
  id: string;
  line: number;
  section: string;
  text: string;
}

function hit(text: string, pats: RegExp[]): string | null {
  for (const p of pats) {
    const m = text.match(p);
    if (m) return m[0];
  }
  return null;
}

27:- **Issuer control:** Existing issuer controls are preserved and extended to confidential balances, including issuer-initiated freezing and clawback that burns the clawed-back funds.

43:- Enhanced Issuer Control: Provides optional Freeze and a Clawback transaction, giving issuers the tools needed to manage assets and enforce compliance. Clawback burns the holder’s confidential balance.
56:  - **AND-composed compact sigma proofs** (referred to as _compact sigma proofs_ throughout this document): proofs that AND-compose multiple ZK statements under a single Fiat–Shamir challenge into a single fixed-size proof per transaction type, bundling ciphertext consistency, amount linkage, and balance linkage checks.
60:  - **Inbox (CB_IN):** Receives incoming transfers and must be explicitly merged into `CB_S`, preventing stale-proof rejection.

The burned funds are permanently removed from circulation.
70:- ConfidentialMPTConvert: Converts public MPT balances into encrypted form for a holder.

114:- **compact sigma proofs**: Cryptographic proofs that bundle multiple ZK statements into a single fixed-size blob verified in one pass. Each transaction uses a dedicated sigma proof optimized for its specific set of hidden values.

Critically, it intentionally reuses the ElGamal ciphertext randomness as its blinding factor rather than introducing an independent scalar, which means the relationship between the commitment and the ciphertexts is captured directly within the compact sigma proof, eliminating the need for a separate amount-linkage proof.
119:  - **Compact ConvertBack sigma proof (128 bytes)**: Used in `ConfidentialMPTConvertBack`. Proves the holder owns the spending balance and that their balance commitment is correctly derived from it.
120:  - **Compact Clawback sigma proof (64 bytes)**: Used in `ConfidentialMPTClawback`. Proves the issuer's on-ledger encrypted balance mirror contains the plaintext amount being claimed.
121:- **Plaintext–ciphertext equality (deterministic):** In `ConfidentialMPTConvert` and `ConfidentialMPTConvertBack`, the disclosed blinding factor allows validators to verify ciphertexts deterministically without a ZKP.
124:  - **Single Bulletproof (688 bytes)**: Used in `ConfidentialMPTConvertBack`. Proves the remaining balance after withdrawal is non-negative.
128:The issuer may designate one or more **delegate accounts** to act on its behalf, for example, to submit `ConfidentialMPTClawback` transactions or to manage the dedicated account (Confidential Vault). Delegate accounts must be considered **fully trusted** by the issuer. A delegate account has complete operational authority within the scope delegated to it, and the protocol does not impose additional on-chain restrictions on delegate actions beyond those that apply to the issuer itself. Issuers should apply the same key-management standards to delegate accounts as to their primary issuer account.
130:`ConfidentialMPTSend`, `ConfidentialMPTMergeInbox`, `ConfidentialMPTConvertBack`, and `ConfidentialMPTClawback` are delegable. **`ConfidentialMPTConvert` is NOT delegable.** It is the transaction that registers an account's `HolderEncryptionKey`, and that key carries exclusive spending authority over the account's confidential balance — delegating it would let the delegate register a key whose secret it alone controls, and thereby take over the account's confidential funds.

178:Enabling confidentiality is **one-way**. Once `lsfMPTCanHoldConfidentialBalance` is set it cannot be cleared — there is no transaction flag to disable confidential balance on an existing issuance. This guarantees that funds already converted to a confidential state can never be stranded by the capability being turned off underneath them.
213:- Whenever `ΔCOA = 0` and the transaction is one of the five confidential MPT transaction types, both `ΔMPTAmount = 0` and `ΔOA = 0` MUST hold. Besides `ConfidentialMPTSend` and `ConfidentialMPTMergeInbox`, this case also covers a zero-amount `ConfidentialMPTConvert` submitted purely to register a `HolderEncryptionKey`.
235:To support confidential MPTs, the existing `MPToken` ledger object is extended with the fields that hold a holder's confidential balance. 496:**Purpose:** Moves all funds from the inbox balance into the spending balance, then resets the inbox to a canonical encrypted zero (EncZero). This ensures that proofs reference only stable spending balances and prevents staleness from incoming transfers.

NEGATIVE-CLAIMS SCOPE
#!/usr/bin/env bun
/**
 * check-negative-claims.ts — a gate for the sentence shape that has failed
 * three times, twice in a single day.
 *
 *   bun run tools/check-negative-claims.ts
 *
 * ## What this is for
 *
 * `UPSTREAM-FEEDBACK.md` is built almost entirely out of statements of the form
 * *"the source does not say X"* — nothing documents it, no field exists, it is
 * not exported, nobody has called it out. Each one is an assertion about a
 * whole corpus, and each one is falsified by a single search.
 *
 * On 2026-08-26, three graded rows failed exactly this way (E-155, E-156):
 *
 *   U-15  quoted a sentence XLS-0096 has never contained, at any revision.
 *   U-12  said a property was "not called out as a selling point anywhere I
 *         found". The spec states it TWICE, once in wording identical to the
 *         benefit claimed as an original reading.
 *   U-10  said "nothing in the documentation says so" about a dependency the
 *         canonical docs document in two places.
 *
 * ⚠ **The reason this shape survives review is that it does not look like a
 * claim.** A quotation has quotation marks to trigger suspicion. A benchmark
 * number visibly wants a methodology. "Nobody has documented this" reads as
 * modesty, and both a self-review and an external reviewer can slide past it.
 *
 * So the gate is not "review harder". It is: **a row asserting a negative must
 * carry the search that would falsify it, in the row.**
 *
 * ## What counts as a falsifier
 *
 * A recorded search a later reader can re-run or check: a `grep`/`rg` command,
 * an explicit occurrence count ("0 occurrences", "zero matches"), a named file
 * plus line, or a dated check against a named source. Prose confidence is not a
 * falsifier. Neither is a grade.
 *
 * ## Scope, and why `Observed` is exempt
 *
 * `CLAUDE.md` requires `Observed` rows to be captured at the moment of friction,
 * ungraded and unresearched — demanding a falsifier there would fight the
 * capture rule and lose. The gate therefore binds the sections where a claim has
 * passed the bar: anything Filed, Ready to file, graded, or offered as Positive.
 * `Observed` rows are reported as advisory only.
 *
 * ⚠ **This gate reports a number, and E-141 is the standing warning that a gate
 * reporting a number is making a claim about what the number counts.** Its own
 * detection is therefore pinned by SELF_TESTS below, which run before it will
 * report anything. If the detectors break, this exits non-zero without grading
 * a single row.
 */

import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

/**
 * Phrases that assert something is absent from a corpus.
 *
 * ⚠ **Each pattern is PAIRED with a probe string that only it should match.**
 * An earlier version kept the patterns in a bare list and self-tested them
 * against whole sentences; breaking one pattern did not fail the tests, because
 * a second pattern matched the same sentence. That is a false-pass mode in the
 * gate's own test — `CLAUDE.md`'s round-two lesson, reproduced here at the cost
 * of one revert. Pairing each pattern with its own probe is what makes a broken
 * detector detectable.
 */
const NEGATIVE_MARKERS: { pattern: RegExp; probe: string }[] = [
  { pattern: /\bnothing (?:in|about|says|said|forces|prevents|collects)\b/i, probe: "nothing in the docs" },
  { pattern: /\bno (?:mention|such field|corresponding|error|warning|counterpart|way|canonical|published|separate)\b/i, probe: "there is no mention" },
  { pattern: /\bnot (?:called out|advertised|documented|exported|stated|specified|published|surfaced|mentioned)\b/i, probe: "it is not advertised" },

BUILD CLAIMS TABLE RENDER
      section,
      summary: summarise(claim),
      grade: summarise(grade, 22) || "—",
    });
  }
  return out;
}

  const bySection = new Map<string, Entry[]>();
  for (const e of entries) {
    if (!bySection.has(e.section)) bySection.set(e.section, []);

    "excerpt for finding things. **The row is the authority** — never cite the index.",
    "",
    `**${entries.length} rows** across **${bySection.size} sections**, counted where they are parsed.`,
    "",
  ];
  for (const [section, rows] of bySection) {
    L.push(`## ${section} — ${rows.length} rows`, "");
    L.push("| id | summary | grade |", "|---|---|---|");
    for (const e of rows) {
      L.push(`| [${e.id}](../CLAIMS.md#L${e.line}) | ${e.summary} | ${e.grade} |`);
    }
    L.push("");
  }
  return L.join("\n");
}

BLOG FIRST DEFINITIONS
    35	The XRP Ledger is public: anyone can read every account and every transaction.
    36	Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs, XLS-33) are one of its token types: an account issues
    37	a token, and other accounts hold it. XLS-96, Confidential Transfers for MPTs, lets
    38	a holder keep an MPT balance encrypted on that public ledger.
    39	
    40	Each confidential balance is an ElGamal ciphertext, a public-key encryption of the
    41	amount. A holder registers their own encryption key when they opt in. The ledger
    42	still has to stop anyone spending more than they hold, so every transaction that
    43	spends from a confidential balance carries zero-knowledge proofs, which validators
    44	check without learning the amount.
    45	
    46	A position moves through four transactions:
    47	
    48	- **Convert** moves tokens from a public balance into the holder's confidential
    49	  inbox. The amount is published.
    50	- **Send** moves an amount from one confidential balance into another holder's
    51	  inbox. The amount is hidden. The sender and receiver are not.
    52	- **MergeInbox** moves the inbox into the balance the holder can spend. Tokens in
    53	  the inbox cannot be sent until they are merged.
    54	- **ConvertBack** moves tokens back to a public balance. The amount is published.
    55	
    56	Only Send hides an amount.
    57	
    58	The specification, XLS-0096, is the work of Murat Cenk, Aanchal Malhotra, Ayo
    59	Akinyele, Peter Chen, Shawn Xie and Yinyi Qian, and has been `Final` since
    60	2026-09-03 (E-1). The compact sigma protocol, the zero-knowledge proof behind a
    61	Send, is the work of Tess Dore and Murat Cenk at RippleX Research. The reference
    62	cryptography is [`XRPLF/mpt-crypto`](https://github.com/XRPLF/mpt-crypto). This
    63	project builds on their work and claims none of it.
    64	
    65	Upstream's code has had three outside reviews. None of them reviewed this
    66	project, which has had no outside audit. Trail of Bits reviewed upstream's
    67	Confidential Transfer implementation in April 2026; that report is the one I could
    68	read and check my findings against, and a later revision of it could not be
    69	obtained. The Sherlock XRP Ledger Attackathon was a contest that covered
    70	Confidential Transfers, and its findings are not public. A Zellic scan of
    71	mpt-crypto is known to me only through three identifiers an upstream issue cites.
    72	Of the three, only Trail of Bits' April report could be checked.

    27	  * 4 resolved in September (spec corrections incorporated into final XLS-96; English documentation corrected regarding zero-balance indistinguishability).
    28	  * 1 build fix (`mpt-crypto` OpenSSL dependency pinning) merged to main on 2026-10-21, awaiting release.
    29	  * 1 pull request approved to expose the zero-encryption calculation in JavaScript/WASM, awaiting merge.
    30	  * 3 issues filed on 2026-10-18 against `mpt-crypto` (nonce scope ambiguity, toolchain build failure, proof size calculation discrepancy) awaiting responses.
    31	  * 1 architectural question to XRPL-Standards regarding vault accounting, unanswered after 57 days.
    32	  * 1 "positives-only" issue closed immediately by `rippled` maintainers for failing to use bug report templates.
    33	* **What the three reviews of the code are:**  
    34	  Here the post fails the reader through ambiguous phrasing. Under the heading *"What went upstream"*, the post states *"Three reviews of this code exist"*, referring to external audits of *upstream/XRPLF code*: (1) Trail of Bits' April 2026 report, (2) the Sherlock XRP Ledger Attackathon, and (3) a Zellic scan of `mpt-crypto`. Conversely, reviews of the author’s *own* project code were not traditional audits at all; they were automated review rounds conducted by other AI models (Codex, Gemini) and separate Claude sessions across 61 internal review records.
    35	
    36	---
    37	
    38	### 3. Where you got lost
    39	
    40	* **Terms used before explained, or never explained:**
    41	  * `"Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs, XLS-33) are one of its token types."`  
    42	    *MPT* is never explained. A reader unfamiliar with XRPL does not know what an MPT is, what properties it has, or how it differs from standard issued currencies.
    43	  * `"Each confidential balance is an ElGamal ciphertext."`  
    44	    *ElGamal ciphertext* is introduced without explaining that ElGamal is an asymmetric encryption scheme that supports public-key encryption and dual-recipient encryption (which explains why the issuer can also decrypt it).
    45	  * `"Tess Dore and Murat Cenk's compact sigma protocol"` / `"The compact sigma protocol behind its send proof..."`  
    46	    *Sigma protocol* is never defined or explained as the underlying zero-knowledge proof technique.
    47	  * `"- MergeInbox moves what a holder has received into the balance they can spend."`  
    48	    The concept of an "inbox" is never introduced before this bullet. A reader does not know why incoming funds land in a distinct inbox rather than directly into the spendable balance, nor why a separate transaction is required to merge them.
    49	  * `"If the token allows clawback, the issuer can destroy it..."`  
    50	    *Clawback* is used without clarifying that it is an XRPL-specific token feature allowing issuers to unilaterally seize or revoke balances.
    51	  * `"A Dedicated Account, an ordinary XRPL account, holds the float..."`  
    52	    Capitalized as if *Dedicated Account* is an XRPL protocol primitive or smart contract type, rather than merely an operational convention chosen by the author.
    53	  * `"A tec result is applied to the ledger. ... a plain Payment that fails with tecNO_AUTH:"`  
    54	    *tec* and *tecNO_AUTH* are completely unexplained. A newcomer has no idea that `tec` represents an XRPL transaction engine error code that still consumes fees and mutates ledger state.
    55	  * `"...whether a confidential balance is meant to stay invisible to vault accounting..."`  
    56	    *Vault accounting* is introduced out of nowhere with zero context as to what vaults are on the XRPL.
    57	
    58	* **Sentences read twice:**
    59	  * `"Read on 2026-10-22 at 03:25 UTC, its amendment, ConfidentialTransfer, was enabled on Devnet, and supported but not enabled on Mainnet and Testnet."`  
    60	    The opening participle "Read on..." reads awkwardly like an instruction or truncated sentence before you realize it means "As observed on...".
    61	  * `"Three reviews of this code exist. Trail of Bits' April 2026 report is the one I could read and check my findings against; a later revision of it could not be obtained."`  
    62	    The antecedent of "this code" is thoroughly confusing. Having just discussed the author's own project and upstream repositories, it sounds like Trail of Bits reviewed the author's project, when it actually reviewed upstream `mpt-crypto`.
    63	  * `"One fails when an observation filed or graded for upstream says a source does not say something, without the search recorded beside it."`  
    64	    The layered double-negatives and internal jargon ("graded for upstream", "says a source does not say something") require multiple passes to parse.
    65	
    66	* **Anything in the wrong order:**
    67	  * **Placement of upstream audit mentions:** The paragraph discussing the Trail of Bits, Sherlock, and Zellic reviews is buried at the end of *"What went upstream"*. It belongs either in an introductory background section on XLS-96 or clearly segregated from the section *"What the reviews caught"*, which discussed AI reviews of the author's code.
    68	  * **Error handling / `tec` failure risks:** The critical privacy revelation—that failed `tec` transactions permanently publish ciphertexts encrypted to bad recipient keys on-ledger—is placed under *"Reading the specification, and running it"* rather than under *"What it hides, and what it does not"*.
    69

    71	
    72	### 4. Where it reads stronger than it should
    73	
    74	* **Misleading impressions of security, audits, and privacy:**
    75	  * *"Three reviews of this code exist. Trail of Bits' April 2026 report is the one I could read and check my findings against..."*  
    76	    Calling upstream libraries *"this code"* strongly implies that the author's codebase has been audited by Trail of Bits, Sherlock, and Zellic.
    77	  * *"Design decisions and fixes went through rounds of adversarial review."*  
    78	    The term *"adversarial review"* strongly connotes formal third-party security audits, red-teaming, or penetration testing, rather than automated prompting across LLM sessions (Claude, Codex, Gemini).
    79	  * *"It hides the shape of the book, not its size."*  
    80	    In credit facilities, the "shape of the book" includes the network graph: who the borrower counterparties are, when they borrow, and borrowing frequency. Because all counterparties, transaction timestamps, and activity patterns are public, the facility only hides the *values/amounts*, not the structural shape of borrowing activity.
    81	
    82	* **Direct contradictions:**
    83	  * **Audited status:**  
    84	    *Sentence 1:* `*Status, before anything else: this is a research project on the XRP Ledger's Devnet test network. It is not audited, not production-ready, and not safe to put value behind.*`  
    85	    *Sentence 2:* `Three reviews of this code exist. Trail of Bits' April 2026 report is the one I could read and check my findings against; a later revision of it could not be obtained.`
    86	  * **What "shape of the book" means:**  
    87	    *Sentence 1:* `It hides the shape of the book, not its size.`  
    88	    *Sentence 2:* `Which supplier drew, and when, is public.` (reinforced by: `They can see which suppliers enrolled, who drew and repaid, on which days, and how often.`)
    89	  * **Web tier safety and keys:**  
    90	    *Sentence 1:* `The demo is static pages built from one snapshot of Devnet. It signs nothing and holds no keys.`  
    91	    *Sentence 2:* `I had written that a read-only web tier "moves no trust boundary". It added no signing authority. But it re-served, to any local user, data the project protects with file permissions (E-230).` (and: `A hostile process running as the same user can read the encryption secret out of memory.`)

Part 6 — the API binds to loopback, and nothing else
  ✓ every .listen( passes an explicit loopback hostname
  ✓ every `host:` under web/app is a loopback literal
  CONTROL ✓ a DUPLICATE hostname key is caught (the LAST one wins in JS)

Asserted-uncaught — the disclosure below fails if these ever start passing
  CONTROL ✓ ASSERTED UNCAUGHT: an indirect socket path assembled at runtime
  CONTROL ✓ a hostname computed at run time IS caught — part 6 fails closed
  CONTROL ✓ a hostname read from the environment IS caught
  CONTROL ✓ a LAN hostname ARGUMENT is caught even when a loopback CONSTANT is present
  CONTROL ✓ a Bun.serve( bind is seen, not only .listen(
  CONTROL ✓ ASSERTED UNCAUGHT: a socket reached through a dependency this gate does not read

  What this gate does NOT say:
    1. It is LEXICAL. A socket path assembled at runtime — string concatenation, an array join, a base64 blob — is invisible to it, and that shape is an asserted-uncaught control above.
    2. It reads THIS REPOSITORY'S sources only. A dependency under node_modules that opens a socket is not read, and could not be gated this way; the property there is that nothing in web/app has a reason to call one.
    3. The needle sets are NAMED. A signing helper spelled differently from every entry in SIGNING_NEEDLES is not counted, by name (E-142's narrowing, forced three times since).
    4. It checks SOURCE, not behaviour. It cannot prove that the one socket client sends only what it constructs, and it is not a substitute for reading that file.
    5. It says nothing about what the tier DISCLOSES. Whether a rendered sentence about privacy is true is `claims-check`'s question and the wording tests', not this gate's.
    6. Part 4 is about what the tier HOLDS; parts 1-3 are about what it can REACH. Those are different properties and the gate had only the second when an issuer key was added to the API process (E-212). A secret obtained some way this list does not name is still invisible.
    7. The signing pass BLANKS string literals, so a call assembled as a string and eval'd is invisible to it. That is the price of not treating prose about another project's API as a violation of ours, it is a deliberate trade, and the socket pass — where a literal IS the value — keeps literals for exactly the opposite reason (CLAIMS.md E-203, fourth consumer).
    8. It scans web/app and web/api ONLY. A signing helper, a socket client or a listener placed in any OTHER directory under web/ — a new web/bridge/, say — is not read at all, and the count in Part 5 is over the two directories it loads (REVIEW-036b).
    9. It does not check for MUTATING routes. A .post, .put or .delete that writes is invisible to every part; 'read-only' is checked as 'reaches no signing operation and holds no secret', which is not the same property (REVIEW-036b).
    10. Part 6's bind check is LEXICAL and FAILS CLOSED. It resolves a quoted literal, or ONE level of indirection to a constant declared in the same source set; anything else — an env read, a ternary, a concatenation, a call — is REFUSED rather than assumed loopback. ⚠ It reads `.listen(` and `Bun.serve(` by name: a listener started through some other API, or in a directory this gate does not load, is invisible (REVIEW-037 F2).
    11. ⚠ Part 6's resolver IGNORES LEXICAL SCOPE. A parameter or inner binding that SHADOWS an outer loopback constant resolves to the outer one, so `function start(HOST){ listen({hostname: HOST}) }` called with a routable address passes. Full scope analysis needs a parser; this is a named limit, not an oversight (REVIEW-037 spot-check, E-238).
    12. ⚠ Part 6 matches `.listen(` and `Bun.serve(` BY NAME. A parenthesised `(Bun.serve)(…)`, a bind through a framework helper, or an aliased reference is invisible. Chasing spellings is how a named set pretends to be a property; it is disclosed instead (E-238).
    13. ⚠ A socket reached through an ALIASED dynamic import — `const t = await import(x); t.connect(…)` with the specifier assembled at run time — is invisible. The import spellings are matched; the aliasing is not, and cannot be lexically (E-238).
    14. ⚠ Part 6 reads STRING LITERALS as values, so prose containing `host: "0.0.0.0"` inside a quoted string FALSE-FAILS. That is the unsafe direction chosen deliberately: a false-fail is loud and gets fixed, a false-pass is silent (CLAIMS.md E-203's two-consumer lesson).
    15. It says nothing about WHO MAY ASK. The tier serves every route unauthenticated on loopback, and loopback is not uid-scoped — so a datum this gate certifies as reachable-by-design is reachable by any local user. Egress is a third property beside REACH and HOLD, and no part of this gate looks at it (CLAIMS.md E-228, REVIEW-036c U1).

UPSTREAM SPEC HEADER AND MECHANICS
     1	<pre>
     2	    title:  Confidential Transfers for Multi-Purpose Tokens
     3	    description: This amendment introduces Confidential Transfers for Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs) on the XRP Ledger.
     4	    implementation: https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/pull/5860
     5	    author: Murat Cenk <redacted@example.invalid>, Aanchal Malhotra <redacted@example.invalid>, Ayo Akinyele <redacted@example.invalid>, Peter Chen <redacted@example.invalid>, Shawn Xie <redacted@example.invalid>, Yinyi Qian <redacted@example.invalid>

     9	    requires: XLS-33
    10	    created: 2026-01-15
    11	    updated: 2026-09-10
